JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself.
On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV.
The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store.
While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service , Howdy.
Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide.

This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others.

“At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners.
Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent.

Your guide to Netflix, Disney Plus, Hulu and more When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . What is JustWatch? If you’ve ever scoured the internet to find which TV streaming service has a specific film or series available, you might have come across this online guide and smartphone app – one that collates together the title listings for a whole load of content services. JustWatch isn’t a TV streaming service itself, though, and you won’t be able to stream anything from within it – but it does offer a handy place to browse everything that is available to stream elsewhere, meaning you don’t have to check apps individually to find what you’re looking for. Let’s face it: there are a lot of TV streaming services these days. While Netflix and YouTube may still be the dominant players when it comes to online streaming, there’s now a host of competitors taking up our screen time. And in a world where Amazon Prime Video , Disney Plus , HBO , and Hulu and are all packed with programming, with content libraries cycling through different titles every month, it can be hard to keep with what’s actually available. That’s where JustWatch comes in – and for everything you need to know about the platform, you’ll find it all on this page. JustWatch is an online guide that collates the various films, TV series, and other types of programming available on online TV streaming services. There’s a website you can open in any browser, and a smartphone app that’s available on iOS and Android , as well as Fire TV devices . This isn’t a new idea: viewers have flocked to the internet to find out what show or film is landing where for years now, but JustWatch is different in its sheer scale. Rather than simply show what’s streaming on a particular service (in the vein of What’sOnNetflix), JustWatch enables you to skim through over 100 different content libraries to see what’s available where, what quality resolution it’s streaming in, how much it costs, and the kind of payment options available (subscription, rental, etc). sources.title: Streaming guide JustWatch becomes a streamer itself
passages: JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself.
On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV.
The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store.
While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service , Howdy.
Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide.

This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others.

“At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners.
Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent.

extraction.body: JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself. On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV. The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store. The media and entertainment company behind the streaming guide, the JustWatch Group, initially announced its plans to venture into streaming last month. At the time, it said partners like Paramount, New Regency, Fremantle, Bleecker Street, and Vortex Media were on board. The company has since announced other content partners, including Cineverse in the U.S., LEONINE Studios in Germany, SND in France, and Altitude in the U.K. The 12-year-old company has long been known for its online guide to movies and TV. Essentially, it’s a “TV Guide” for the streaming era, helping users navigate a landscape where movies and shows move from one service to another, making it harder to keep up with what’s streaming where. Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide. This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others. Now the company believes there’s an even bigger opportunity to grow its audience data and insights by running its own service. “At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners. This is a natural continuation of our mission to contribute to the entire ecosystem, from the big screen to the small one.” The new streaming service will be available within JustWatch’s existing apps and website across 12 markets, including the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Ireland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Australia, and New Zealand. Its free tier will offer a selection of ad-supported titles, while the ad-free version, JustWatch TV Plus, will offer more than 300 ad-free titles in the U.S., as well as other exclusive features, like advanced filters and the option to hide previously seen or disliked titles in the guide. A movie rental store will also initially be available in the U.S., U.K., Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, with more markets to follow in time. While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service , Howdy. It will be similarly priced at $3.99 per month or $49.99 for a lifetime subscription. (The latter is an interesting way to price streaming, given the evolving content costs, but JustWatch believes there will be additional value in the data collected.) Paid subscribers will also be able to take 10% off on hundreds of rentals in the JustWatch TV Store, the company noted. Like most low-cost services, JustWatch’s content lineup focuses on older movies and shows, as well as more indie content. Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent. JustWatch says users will be able to request titles they want to see to help shape what comes to the service. However, if you want to watch something epic without dishing out the big bucks, then free streamers like Hoopla , Plex , and Pluto will be your best bet.
To take out some of the guesswork that follows, here are the 10 best fantasy movies streaming for free right now.
Movies are the best type of escapism, and when you truly want to disappear into a fictional world for a bit, no genre is better than fantasy.
However, the next question becomes how do you watch them on streaming.
The movie follows one unicorn's desperate search to discover what happened to the rest of her species, and what follows is a story packed with themes about mortality, existential fear, and regret.
For these reasons, it's best suited for older kids and adults.
This isn't My Little Pony (1986), meaning young children might have difficulty processing these mature themes despite the G-rating.

The costume and set designs are actually quite impressive.
Plus, Frank Langella is having one heck of a good time playing Skeletor.
With a new He-Man film slated for release in June 2026, it's the perfect time to revisit the first live-action adaptation of Mattel's favorite toyline hero turned movie and TV star.
44 other streaming services also have titles available to stream today.

Monty Python and the Holy Grail isn't the movie to watch when you're craving a serious fantasy movie.
Told in a non-linear fashion with some genuinely impressive transitions between time periods, the movie offers a compelling time-travel story steeped in action and fantasy.
The proof is in the pudding, with director Matteo Garrone—a lifelong fan of Carlo Collodi's original fairy tale—producing a critically acclaimed, award-winning film.
The daydreaming sequences are fun, whimsical, and utterly theatrical.

More importantly, the film delves into a topic we can all relate to: the desire for escapism that often creeps up when life gets too boring and mundane.

extraction.body: J.P. Morgan announced on October 19 that its Kinexys business had brought JPM Coin (JPMD), its US dollar-denominated deposit token, to Ethereum mainnet for institutional clients. Confirmed in a company announcement , the deployment expands JPM Coin’s availability beyond Base, giving approved participants another public blockchain for moving tokenized deposits. JPM Coin remains a permissioned product restricted to approved institutional participants rather than a retail-accessible crypto asset, according to Cointelegraph. The Ethereum deployment places JPM Coin on the network where a broad range of assets, collateral arrangements and counterparties already operate onchain. It gives clients another public-chain option for near-real-time, around-the-clock money movement, according to Bloomberg Law . JPM Coin is denominated in US dollars and represents deposits within J.P. Morgan’s system. The announcement concerns its availability on Ethereum mainnet for institutional clients; it does not signal an opening of the token to the general public. J.P. Morgan said JPM Coin supports peer-to-peer transfers between institutional clients in the Ethereum Virtual Machine ecosystem, including Ethereum and Base. The bank described the arrangement as an onchain liquidity layer for USD deposits. That framing focuses on settlement between eligible institutions operating across those networks. Access is restricted to approved institutional participants, a limitation reported by Cointelegraph , rather than an unrestricted token offering on Ethereum. The Ethereum rollout follows JPM Coin’s November 2025 launch on Base. The expansion brings the bank’s deposit-token infrastructure to a second public blockchain while retaining the approved-participant model. Kinexys has processed more than $4 trillion in cumulative transactions since inception and has averaged $7 billion in daily transaction volume, according to J.P. Morgan. sources.title: JPMorgan brings deposit token to ethereum for institutional clients - The Edge Malaysia
passages: JPM Coin — which represents US dollar deposits at the largest US bank — will be made available to the company’s institutional clients on the ethereum network, JPMorgan said in a statement on Monday.

First launched last year on Coinbase Global Inc-affiliated blockchain base, the deposit token allows clients to send and receive money in seconds and 24/7, rather than over several days and only during working hours.
The bank chose to bring the token to ethereum because of its liquidity and existing use among clients, Landriault said.
JPMorgan is one of the more active banks in blockchain development.
It also runs the Kinexys Blockchain Deposit Account network, which allows corporate clients to move dollars, euros, pounds and several other currencies, on the bank’s private blockchain.
The network processes more than US$7 billion in transactions a day, JPMorgan said, a sliver of the roughly US$12 trillion a day its broader payments division handles daily.
(Oct 19): JPMorgan Chase & Co is launching its deposit token on ethereum, extending the lender’s push into blockchain payments as Wall Street grows more comfortable moving money on public networks.
JPMorgan’s expansion comes as banks and other large financial firms seek ways to move assets faster and beyond the limitations of traditional systems by using crypto’s underlying technology.
A company backed by more than 100 corporations including Visa Inc, Stripe Inc, and Mastercard Inc issued a US dollar-pegged stablecoin last month, another form of digital money.

“It’s not just Wall Street going to public chains, but the institutional web3 players getting more embedded and partnering with traditional financial institutions.” JPM Coin’s move onto ethereum underscores that shift, she added.

Moving onto public infrastructure — albeit with limits on who can hold the tokens — brings Wall Street closer to the crypto ecosystem, enabling them to tap into existing pools of liquidity and developer activity.

passages: JPM Coin — which represents US dollar deposits at the largest US bank — will be made available to the company’s institutional clients on the ethereum network, JPMorgan said in a statement on Monday.

First launched last year on Coinbase Global Inc-affiliated blockchain base, the deposit token allows clients to send and receive money in seconds and 24/7, rather than over several days and only during working hours.
The bank chose to bring the token to ethereum because of its liquidity and existing use among clients, Landriault said.
JPMorgan is one of the more active banks in blockchain development.
It also runs the Kinexys Blockchain Deposit Account network, which allows corporate clients to move dollars, euros, pounds and several other currencies, on the bank’s private blockchain.
The network processes more than US$7 billion in transactions a day, JPMorgan said, a sliver of the roughly US$12 trillion a day its broader payments division handles daily.
(Oct 19): JPMorgan Chase & Co is launching its deposit token on ethereum, extending the lender’s push into blockchain payments as Wall Street grows more comfortable moving money on public networks.
JPMorgan’s expansion comes as banks and other large financial firms seek ways to move assets faster and beyond the limitations of traditional systems by using crypto’s underlying technology.
A company backed by more than 100 corporations including Visa Inc, Stripe Inc, and Mastercard Inc issued a US dollar-pegged stablecoin last month, another form of digital money.

“It’s not just Wall Street going to public chains, but the institutional web3 players getting more embedded and partnering with traditional financial institutions.” JPM Coin’s move onto ethereum underscores that shift, she added.

Moving onto public infrastructure — albeit with limits on who can hold the tokens — brings Wall Street closer to the crypto ecosystem, enabling them to tap into existing pools of liquidity and developer activity.

extraction.body: Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it investigates its privacy. Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. Every time a webpage loads, the internet's address-lookup system logs which hostname was requested. Passive-DNS providers retain those historical observations, making hostnames associated with a domain searchable long after the original request. The risk applied specifically to conversations users had deliberately shared through the feature, while unintended discoverability was the reported problem. Private sessions operated separately, according to Meta's documentation describing isolated cloud environments . Muse is built to sit across your entire digital life, and that reach creates multiple data paths: private sessions, sharing features, connected-account integrations, and more. Think of it like a smart thermostat that also controls your front-door camera. The device itself may be secure, but each integration deserves its own scrutiny. Treat any AI share link as potentially discoverable by secretly tracking users and infrastructure outside your control. Delete shared pages when the conversation has served its purpose, where deletion controls are available, and evaluate each sharing or integration feature on its own terms to stay safe . For some, blunders and privacy scares from their agents have proven too unnerving. Four early adopters, among dozens of people raising similar concerns on social media, told Business Insider they had deleted or restricted personal AI agents over concerns about the sensitive data and account access the tools need to work effectively. Guto Martino, a cofounder of Hermes Agents Brasil, a community that helps people build and run open-source personal AI agents, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct because he was unsure how the company handled his information. "I have no clue where my data is going and what kind of privacy I do get from using that agent," Martino said. Martino's decision follows a string of troubling episodes involving personal AI agents. Users have reported agents accessing one-time login codes from Gmail without asking, hallucinating personal information from a document that was never sent, and triggering a carrier-account login prompt apparently originating from Iran. Meta said Muse has "first-of-its-kind privacy, safety, and security protections" and that its controls put users in charge of what they share. It said users choose which apps Muse connects to and what it can do with services such as email, and can change or remove access, or permanently delete their Muse data. While a handful of users are wary, vastly more are experimenting with the technology. Muse shot to the top of the App Store a week after launch, and it continues to attract users. The Information reported that Meta's Muse now has more than 3 million weekly users, including more than 1 million daily active users. But Shinn said on an episode of "Invest Like The Best" in late September that the invite-only service has been growing by roughly 10% a day and is processing more than $1 billion in annualized transaction volume, despite what he called a "very small user base." But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information. Scott Persinger, the CTO of AI-powered travel platform BizTrip, told Business Insider he found Instinct "very cool," but deleted it because he was not prepared to let a young startup handle his personal email. "Access to email is everything — via password resets you could probably access my whole life," he said. He said he still uses Meta's Muse and xAI's Grok Bot, though neither is connected to his inbox. "I fully expect to use a personal assistant with my email," Persinger said. "But I want to hear someone describe how they built it safely, not just 'yolo — trust us.'" Muse users weren't spared. Rami Elghandour, chairman and CEO of Arcellx, a clinical-stage biotechnology company, told Business Insider he deleted Muse after reading reports that the agent had accessed users' text messages without permission. Elghandour had used Muse to search for a new Mac Studio and a car, but said he had deliberately not connected it to any accounts or personal data. "The fact that it was accessing user text messages without their consent was alarming but not surprising given it's Meta," Elghandour said. "I certainly did not grant or would I ever grant access to all my messages to Meta." He said he instead uses an agent he built himself with an open-source model on a Mac Mini, which has access to his email, calendar, and messages. "I’m not sure I would give that level of access to any company," he said. Deleted Muse after seeing this post on Threads about how it told some Facebook Marketplace sellers the guy’s address and they showed up at his doorDangerous and creepyThis would have been 1000x worse if the person was a woman pic.twitter.com/KQbkwRzDPt For others, the potential for data leaks was the last straw. Mahesh Vellanki, the founder and CEO of YieldClub, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct after it triggered a two-factor authentication request from an IP location labeled as Iran while trying to log into his carrier account. He said Instinct suggested it could have been a benign IP-tagging issue, and he could not establish that its systems were compromised. Still, the episode left him feeling "very exposed." Vellanki said he still uses personal AI agents, but no longer gives them sensitive information. "More just using them generally, but not giving them full keys to the castle," he said. "It’s the wild west with these products," he added. Not every early user worried about their personal data has chosen to abandon personal AI agents. Rishi Bhargava, cofounder of Descope, said he is experimenting with Muse and Instinct but has been "very careful" about the access he gives them, including by withholding his passwords. He said he uses Instinct only for lower-stakes tasks, such as search and research. "The interface is extremely convenient, and I like the asynchronous nature of it," he said. But Bhargava said companies behind personal AI agents have not adequately explained how they handle and protect personal data. Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them. It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.

"But I want to hear someone describe how they built it safely, not just 'yolo — trust us.'" Muse users weren't spared.

Rami Elghandour, chairman and CEO of Arcellx, a clinical-stage biotechnology company, told Business Insider he deleted Muse after reading reports that the agent had accessed users' text messages without permission.
Elghandour had used Muse to search for a new Mac Studio and a car, but said he had deliberately not connected it to any accounts or personal data.
"The fact that it was accessing user text messages without their consent was alarming but not surprising given it's Meta," Elghandour said.

"I certainly did not grant or would I ever grant access to all my messages to Meta." He said he instead uses an agent he built himself with an open-source model on a Mac Mini, which has access to his email, calendar, and messages.
"I’m not sure I would give that level of access to any company," he said.

Deleted Muse after seeing this post on Threads about how it told some Facebook Marketplace sellers the guy’s address and they showed up at his doorDangerous and creepyThis would have been 1000x worse if the person was a woman pic.twitter.com/KQbkwRzDPt For others, the potential for data leaks was the last straw.

Mahesh Vellanki, the founder and CEO of YieldClub, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct after it triggered a two-factor authentication request from an IP location labeled as Iran while trying to log into his carrier account.

"More just using them generally, but not giving them full keys to the castle," he said.
"It’s the wild west with these products," he added.
Not every early user worried about their personal data has chosen to abandon personal AI agents.
Rishi Bhargava, cofounder of Descope, said he is experimenting with Muse and Instinct but has been "very careful" about the access he gives them, including by withholding his passwords.
He said he uses Instinct only for lower-stakes tasks, such as search and research.
"The interface is extremely convenient, and I like the asynchronous nature of it," he said.
But Bhargava said companies behind personal AI agents have not adequately explained how they handle and protect personal data.
Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them.
It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.

“What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search.

extraction.body: Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it investigates its privacy. Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: “If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.” In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said: We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered. Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way. The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database. Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible. “Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.” Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended. Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires. With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said:

We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.

Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way.

The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database.

Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible.

“Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.”

Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended.

Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires.
With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now.

With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

sources.title: Early users delete personal AI agents over privacy scares and blunders
passages: But Shinn said on an episode of "Invest Like The Best" in late September that the invite-only service has been growing by roughly 10% a day and is processing more than $1 billion in annualized transaction volume, despite what he called a "very small user base." But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information.
For some, blunders and privacy scares from their agents have proven too unnerving.

Four early adopters, among dozens of people raising similar concerns on social media, told Business Insider they had deleted or restricted personal AI agents over concerns about the sensitive data and account access the tools need to work effectively.

Users have reported agents accessing one-time login codes from Gmail without asking, hallucinating personal information from a document that was never sent, and triggering a carrier-account login prompt apparently originating from Iran.
"I have no clue where my data is going and what kind of privacy I do get from using that agent," Martino said.
Meta said Muse has "first-of-its-kind privacy, safety, and security protections" and that its controls put users in charge of what they share.
It said users choose which apps Muse connects to and what it can do with services such as email, and can change or remove access, or permanently delete their Muse data.
It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.
Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them.

Many early adopters of Instinct and Meta's Muse have said the digital assistants saved them time and money by searching the web, managing inboxes and calendars, disputing bills, booking travel, and making purchases.
Muse shot to the top of the App Store a week after launch, and it continues to attract users.
"But I want to hear someone describe how they built it safely, not just 'yolo — trust us.'" Muse users weren't spared.
Elghandour had used Muse to search for a new Mac Studio and a car, but said he had deliberately not connected it to any accounts or personal data.

For some, blunders and privacy scares from their agents have proven too unnerving. Four early adopters, among dozens of people raising similar concerns on social media, told Business Insider they had deleted or restricted personal AI agents over concerns about the sensitive data and account access the tools need to work effectively. Guto Martino, a cofounder of Hermes Agents Brasil, a community that helps people build and run open-source personal AI agents, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct because he was unsure how the company handled his information. "I have no clue where my data is going and what kind of privacy I do get from using that agent," Martino said. Martino's decision follows a string of troubling episodes involving personal AI agents. Users have reported agents accessing one-time login codes from Gmail without asking, hallucinating personal information from a document that was never sent, and triggering a carrier-account login prompt apparently originating from Iran. Meta said Muse has "first-of-its-kind privacy, safety, and security protections" and that its controls put users in charge of what they share. It said users choose which apps Muse connects to and what it can do with services such as email, and can change or remove access, or permanently delete their Muse data. While a handful of users are wary, vastly more are experimenting with the technology. Muse shot to the top of the App Store a week after launch, and it continues to attract users. The Information reported that Meta's Muse now has more than 3 million weekly users, including more than 1 million daily active users. But Shinn said on an episode of "Invest Like The Best" in late September that the invite-only service has been growing by roughly 10% a day and is processing more than $1 billion in annualized transaction volume, despite what he called a "very small user base." But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information. Scott Persinger, the CTO of AI-powered travel platform BizTrip, told Business Insider he found Instinct "very cool," but deleted it because he was not prepared to let a young startup handle his personal email. "Access to email is everything — via password resets you could probably access my whole life," he said. He said he still uses Meta's Muse and xAI's Grok Bot, though neither is connected to his inbox. "I fully expect to use a personal assistant with my email," Persinger said. "But I want to hear someone describe how they built it safely, not just 'yolo — trust us.'" Muse users weren't spared. Rami Elghandour, chairman and CEO of Arcellx, a clinical-stage biotechnology company, told Business Insider he deleted Muse after reading reports that the agent had accessed users' text messages without permission. Elghandour had used Muse to search for a new Mac Studio and a car, but said he had deliberately not connected it to any accounts or personal data. "The fact that it was accessing user text messages without their consent was alarming but not surprising given it's Meta," Elghandour said. "I certainly did not grant or would I ever grant access to all my messages to Meta." He said he instead uses an agent he built himself with an open-source model on a Mac Mini, which has access to his email, calendar, and messages. "I’m not sure I would give that level of access to any company," he said. Deleted Muse after seeing this post on Threads about how it told some Facebook Marketplace sellers the guy’s address and they showed up at his doorDangerous and creepyThis would have been 1000x worse if the person was a woman pic.twitter.com/KQbkwRzDPt For others, the potential for data leaks was the last straw. Mahesh Vellanki, the founder and CEO of YieldClub, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct after it triggered a two-factor authentication request from an IP location labeled as Iran while trying to log into his carrier account. He said Instinct suggested it could have been a benign IP-tagging issue, and he could not establish that its systems were compromised. Still, the episode left him feeling "very exposed." Vellanki said he still uses personal AI agents, but no longer gives them sensitive information. "More just using them generally, but not giving them full keys to the castle," he said. "It’s the wild west with these products," he added. Not every early user worried about their personal data has chosen to abandon personal AI agents. Rishi Bhargava, cofounder of Descope, said he is experimenting with Muse and Instinct but has been "very careful" about the access he gives them, including by withholding his passwords. He said he uses Instinct only for lower-stakes tasks, such as search and research. "The interface is extremely convenient, and I like the asynchronous nature of it," he said. But Bhargava said companies behind personal AI agents have not adequately explained how they handle and protect personal data. Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them. It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.

sources.title: Bill Gates says he's ready to plow billions into a next-gen nuclear plant being built by his startup - Fortune
passages: Bill Gates said he’s prepared to plow billions of dollars into a next-generation nuclear power plant project in Wyoming to meet growing US electricity needs.

TerraPower LLC, a startup founded by Gates, broke ground for construction of its first commercial reactor last week in Wyoming, where a coal plant is shutting down, the billionaire co-founder of Microsoft Corp. said on CBS’s Face the Nation .
“I put in over a billion, and I’ll put in billions more,” said Gates, the world’s sixth-richest person according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

extraction.body: Bill Gates said he’s prepared to plow billions of dollars into a next-generation nuclear power plant project in Wyoming to meet growing US electricity needs. TerraPower LLC, a startup founded by Gates, broke ground for construction of its first commercial reactor last week in Wyoming, where a coal plant is shutting down, the billionaire co-founder of Microsoft Corp. said on CBS’s Face the Nation . TerraPower has explored simpler, cheaper reactors since 2008 and expects to complete the new reactor in 2030. “I put in over a billion, and I’ll put in billions more,” said Gates, the world’s sixth-richest person according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. TerraPower’s plant, which has backing by the US Department of Energy, was initially expected to be operational in 2028. But that would have meant relying on fuel from Russia, which is “unacceptable now,” Gates said on CNN’s Fareed Zakaria GPS . The reactor design uses liquid sodium as a coolant rather than water and includes molten salt that can store heat to boost its output. TerraPower plans to source reactor fuel from the US and its allies, Gates said. “Coal is being outcompeted by natural gas,” Gates told CNN. “And so what we have to do is compete effectively with natural gas.” Carbon-free nuclear power is increasingly seen as a key part of fighting climate change, and more companies are promoting smaller reactors. Last year, 25 nations at the COP28 climate change conference in Dubai declared an ambition to triple nuclear capacity, according to BloombergNEF.

TerraPower LLC, a startup founded by Gates, broke ground for construction of its first commercial reactor last week in Wyoming, where a coal plant is shutting down, the billionaire co-founder of Microsoft Corp. said on CBS’s Face the Nation . TerraPower has explored simpler, cheaper reactors since 2008 and expects to complete the new reactor in 2030. “I put in over a billion, and I’ll put in billions more,” said Gates, the world’s sixth-richest person according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. TerraPower’s plant, which has backing by the US Department of Energy, was initially expected to be operational in 2028. But that would have meant relying on fuel from Russia, which is “unacceptable now,” Gates said on CNN’s Fareed Zakaria GPS . The reactor design uses liquid sodium as a coolant rather than water and includes molten salt that can store heat to boost its output. TerraPower plans to source reactor fuel from the US and its allies, Gates said. “Coal is being outcompeted by natural gas,” Gates told CNN. “And so what we have to do is compete effectively with natural gas.” Carbon-free nuclear power is increasingly seen as a key part of fighting climate change, and more companies are promoting smaller reactors. Last year, 25 nations at the COP28 climate change conference in Dubai declared an ambition to triple nuclear capacity, according to BloombergNEF.

passages: 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Aikido Security today announced the launch of Noon , a dedicated workforce security business that extends its protection beyond software to the people using it.
AI has made sophisticated phishing, deepfakes and coordinated social engineering attacks cheaper, easier to execute and more scalable than ever before.
Noon addresses these threats by bringing email protection, device protection, AI governance and phishing simulation training together in one platform.
"We started Aikido to make securing software radically simpler," said Willem Delbare, CEO of Aikido Security.
"But companies don't just need to protect the software they build.
With Noon, we're bringing the same approach to workforce security: one platform, less complexity, and protection for every employee, not just those building software."

Noon's platform is being built on two acquisitions Aikido completed in September 2026: Poland-based Cyberly, founded in 2024, which brought AI-driven attack simulations and AI usage visibility, and Belgium-based Outkept, founded in 2020, which brought email security and phishing awareness training.
Before the acquisitions, Cyberly protected more than 300,000 employees across 200-plus organizations, while Outkept served more than 1,000 organizations and 250,000 users across 100-plus countries.
"AI has fundamentally changed how we need to train and protect employees.
"Joining forces with Cyberly and Aikido gives us the opportunity to rethink workforce security and bring a new generation of protection to organizations of all sizes."
Aikido's unified security platform secures application testing, code, cloud and runtime, helping teams to reduce risk without slowing down development.

Aikido is the fastest-ever European cybersecurity company to reach unicorn status and is trusted by over 150,000 teams, with a global customer base including SoundCloud, Niantic, Runway, Handshake and Deel.
Noon brings employee security into one platform, replacing the separate tools many organizations piece together today:
Aikido Security achieves FedRAMP Moderate Authorization, bringing AI-native, automated vulnerability remediation to U.S. federal agencies.
Yet the security industry has long treated software and workforce security as two separate worlds," said Alex Horlach, co-founder of Cyberly.
The founding teams of both companies continue at Noon.
Cyberly's four co-founders, Alex Horlach, Evgeny Chamtonau, Pavel Hraznykh and Andrew Labadzinski, will continue building the platform.

Together, Cyberly and Outkept bring established international customer relationships and a strong foundation for Noon's growth, with additional opportunities across Aikido's existing customer network.
Most workforce security stacks were built for a different problem: generic phishing emails and scheduled tests.
They also run separately from the tools protecting employee devices or tracking AI usage, leaving security teams managing several disconnected products.
Noon connects directly to Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Slack and Microsoft Teams, and its results are built to feed into GRC platforms.
Campaign and training data is designed to support audits under frameworks including SOC 2, ISO 27001, NIS2, DORA, HIPAA and GDPR, and to help meet cyber insurance requirements.
Aikido achieves AWS Security Competency for Application Security, giving AWS customers independent validation of its code-to-cloud-to-runtime platform.

"We started Aikido to make securing software radically simpler," said Willem Delbare, CEO of Aikido Security. "But companies don't just need to protect the software they build. Phishing used to require research on a target, a convincing personalized message and a fake login page. AI has stripped out the time, skill and cost. At the same time, AI assistants and autonomous workflows have become part of everyday work, with limited visibility for security teams. "Attackers don't always need to break into software when they can simply trick the people using it. But impersonation is only part of it. Employees are installing AI tools, connecting MCP servers, and giving agents access to company systems and data . The proportion of employees who use AI regularly on corporate devices has tripled in one year. Every new tool, package, and agent skill introduces something else to secure.

Protecting your workforce now means understanding what people are installing, what their agents can do, and which tools can access company data. Alongside the inboxes, devices, and people you already needed to protect.
So there’s more to protect, and the attacks look more real. And it’s only getting worse. Much, much worse. AI makes attacks like these easier to create, personalize, and run at scale.

AI has made sophisticated phishing, deepfakes and coordinated social engineering attacks cheaper, easier to execute and more scalable than ever before.
Noon addresses these threats by bringing email protection, device protection, AI governance and phishing simulation training together in one platform.
"We started Aikido to make securing software radically simpler," said Willem Delbare, CEO of Aikido Security.
"But companies don't just need to protect the software they build.

Noon's platform is being built on two acquisitions Aikido completed in September 2026: Poland-based Cyberly, founded in 2024, which brought AI-driven attack simulations and AI usage visibility, and Belgium-based Outkept, founded in 2020, which brought email security and phishing awareness training.
Before the acquisitions, Cyberly protected more than 300,000 employees across 200-plus organizations, while Outkept served more than 1,000 organizations and 250,000 users across 100-plus countries.
"AI has fundamentally changed how we need to train and protect employees.

Noon brings employee security into one platform, replacing the separate tools many organizations piece together today:

Visa has partnered with Mesh to enable crypto and stablecoin spending at more than 175 million merchant locations across over 200 countries and territories. Consumers will be able to pay directly from supported wallet balances without cashing out, transferring funds or obtaining separate payment cards. Mesh will handle transaction funding and conversion, while merchants continue receiving payments through Visa's existing infrastructure. Participating platforms can offer the service through a single Mesh integration, with the company managing onboarding and customer verification. Initial availability, supported devices and participating crypto wallets have yet to be announced. 19 announcement, Mesh said the partnership would connect digital wallets and cryptocurrency platforms to Visa's payment network through its transaction processing infrastructure, allowing users to make purchases directly from their existing balances. The proposed service will support payments at physical stores and online merchants across more than 200 countries and territories where Visa operates. Mesh will handle the conversion and movement of funds behind each transaction, while merchants receive payments through their existing checkout systems. Visa processed $14.2 trillion in payment volume during fiscal 2025, according to figures cited in the announcement. Visa and Mesh will connect crypto wallets to existing payment terminals Under the agreement, Mesh will allow participating wallet providers and cryptocurrency platforms to offer payments directly from digital asset balances without requiring customers to withdraw their holdings before making a purchase. The payment process will rely on a Visa credential created in the background. Mesh will manage the funding and conversion process when a transaction takes place, drawing from supported cryptocurrency, stablecoin or fiat balances. Merchants will continue receiving payments through Visa's existing infrastructure, without installing new hardware or changing how they accept transactions. The arrangement does not mean merchants will receive cryptocurrency directly. Mesh will handle the conversion required to complete payments through the conventional payment network. According to the company, wallet providers can activate the service through a single Mesh integration without developing and operating their own card programs. Mesh will act as the program manager and handle customer onboarding and know your customer checks associated with the service. The company said its network already serves more than 200 enterprises and connects hundreds of wallets, exchanges and financial platforms. Its existing enterprise relationships include Kalshi, Tools for Humanity, Félix Pago, Majority and KAST, although the announcement did not confirm which partners would participate in the initial Visa rollout. "Crypto never had a spending problem, it has a last-mile problem," Mesh co-founder and CEO Bam Azizi said in the announcement. Azizi said the company's infrastructure would manage funding and conversion at the time of payment, removing the need for customers to move money between accounts before making purchases. Visa's global head of growth, Rubail Birwadker, said the collaboration would give consumers more ways to use digital asset balances through established payment services. Visa expands stablecoin payments beyond dedicated card programs The partnership follows several initiatives by Visa to connect cryptocurrency holdings and stablecoin transactions with its existing payments infrastructure. In September, Visa disclosed that more than 160 stablecoin card programs were operating globally during its fiscal second quarter of 2026. Payment volume across those programs had climbed nearly 200% from the previous year, while the company's stablecoin settlement business surpassed an annualized rate of $20 billion. An October update showed that stablecoin card payments continued to record nearly 200% annual growth across Visa's network. Business and commercial programs accounted for approximately 17% of the company's stablecoin-linked card payment volume during fiscal 2026. The Mesh arrangement uses a different customer-facing model from conventional cryptocurrency card programs because participating platforms can provide payment access without requiring customers to obtain a separate card associated with each wallet. Earlier payment integrations have generally required users to convert cryptocurrency into fiat before spending it or rely on dedicated cards issued through specific providers. In January, Visa partnered with Mercuryo to allow eligible users to convert cryptocurrency into fiat and transfer the proceeds to Visa debit and credit cards through Visa Direct. The service was designed to deliver funds to eligible cards within minutes, depending on the supported market and payment conditions. Visa entered another digital asset agreement in October when it partnered with ADI Foundation to explore blockchain infrastructure and digital payment systems. That agreement remained exploratory, with neither company announcing a specific blockchain, stablecoin or commercial launch date. Mesh builds on existing exchange and stablecoin integrations Mesh has spent much of 2026 adding cryptocurrency exchanges, wallets and payment platforms to its network. In September, crypto.news reported that Bybit Pay integrated Mesh to connect its payment service with more than 300 wallets, exchanges and financial platforms.

Visa processed $14.2 trillion in payment volume during fiscal 2025, according to figures cited in the announcement.

Visa and Mesh will connect crypto wallets to existing payment terminals Under the agreement, Mesh will allow participating wallet providers and cryptocurrency platforms to offer payments directly from digital asset balances without requiring customers to withdraw their holdings before making a purchase.
The payment process will rely on a Visa credential created in the background.
Mesh will manage the funding and conversion process when a transaction takes place, drawing from supported cryptocurrency, stablecoin or fiat balances.
Merchants will continue receiving payments through Visa's existing infrastructure, without installing new hardware or changing how they accept transactions.
The arrangement does not mean merchants will receive cryptocurrency directly.
Mesh will handle the conversion required to complete payments through the conventional payment network.
According to the company, wallet providers can activate the service through a single Mesh integration without developing and operating their own card programs.
Mesh will act as the program manager and handle customer onboarding and know your customer checks associated with the service.
The company said its network already serves more than 200 enterprises and connects hundreds of wallets, exchanges and financial platforms.

Its existing enterprise relationships include Kalshi, Tools for Humanity, Félix Pago, Majority and KAST, although the announcement did not confirm which partners would participate in the initial Visa rollout.
"Crypto never had a spending problem, it has a last-mile problem," Mesh co-founder and CEO Bam Azizi said in the announcement.
Azizi said the company's infrastructure would manage funding and conversion at the time of payment, removing the need for customers to move money between accounts before making purchases.
Visa's global head of growth, Rubail Birwadker, said the collaboration would give consumers more ways to use digital asset balances through established payment services.

Visa expands stablecoin payments beyond dedicated card programs The partnership follows several initiatives by Visa to connect cryptocurrency holdings and stablecoin transactions with its existing payments infrastructure.
In September, Visa disclosed that more than 160 stablecoin card programs were operating globally during its fiscal second quarter of 2026.
Payment volume across those programs had climbed nearly 200% from the previous year, while the company's stablecoin settlement business surpassed an annualized rate of $20 billion.
An October update showed that stablecoin card payments continued to record nearly 200% annual growth across Visa's network.
Business and commercial programs accounted for approximately 17% of the company's stablecoin-linked card payment volume during fiscal 2026.

The Mesh arrangement uses a different customer-facing model from conventional cryptocurrency card programs because participating platforms can provide payment access without requiring customers to obtain a separate card associated with each wallet.
Earlier payment integrations have generally required users to convert cryptocurrency into fiat before spending it or rely on dedicated cards issued through specific providers.
In January, Visa partnered with Mercuryo to allow eligible users to convert cryptocurrency into fiat and transfer the proceeds to Visa debit and credit cards through Visa Direct.
The service was designed to deliver funds to eligible cards within minutes, depending on the supported market and payment conditions.
Visa entered another digital asset agreement in October when it partnered with ADI Foundation to explore blockchain infrastructure and digital payment systems.
That agreement remained exploratory, with neither company announcing a specific blockchain, stablecoin or commercial launch date.
Mesh builds on existing exchange and stablecoin integrations Mesh has spent much of 2026 adding cryptocurrency exchanges, wallets and payment platforms to its network.
In September, crypto.news reported that Bybit Pay integrated Mesh to connect its payment service with more than 300 wallets, exchanges and financial platforms.

The company announced this significant development on October 19, 2026. Many crypto holders have never spent their digital assets in stores. Until now, converting crypto to cash often required selling coins, waiting for the funds to transfer to a bank, or signing up for a crypto debit card linked to a specific exchange. While the checkout process is straightforward under this new arrangement, tax considerations can catch new users off guard. Here’s what to expect at checkout and what tax implications may follow. The wallet app takes care of most of the payment process. According to the announcement, the participating wallet app sets up a Visa card behind the scenes. Users can tap a standard contactless terminal or check out online without selling, transferring, or preloading any funds. When it’s time to pay, Mesh determines how the purchase is funded—crypto, a stablecoin (a token designed to maintain a steady $1 value), or regular dollars. The merchant receives the payment as a standard Visa transaction, requiring no additional hardware and ensuring cashiers see a typical card payment. "Fishpool gold coins" by Lawrence OP is licensed under BY 2.0. Mesh has not yet specified which cryptocurrencies it will support, any applicable fees, or which countries it will include in the initial rollout. Users should check their wallet apps to confirm three critical details before buying. The IRS classifies cryptocurrencies as property. As a result, spending crypto is a taxable event, similar to selling it. The IRS states that “an exchange of digital assets for property, goods, or services” constitutes a taxable transaction. According to Form 1040 instructions, you must report any disposal through payment on Form 8949 and Schedule D. For instance, if someone purchases a $1,000 laptop using Bitcoin bought at $500, they owe taxes on the $500 gain , even if they haven’t converted any crypto to cash. At the 15% long-term capital gains rate (for assets held over a year), the laptop adds about $75 to their tax bill. Coins held for a year or less are taxed at the regular income tax rate, which is usually higher. Additionally, a purchase can lock in a loss. For example, if Bitcoin trades at about $81,000 , down from $111,000 a year earlier, selling coins bought at the higher price would realize a capital loss that could offset other capital gains. Stablecoins largely avoid these complexities, as tokens like USD Coin ( CRYPTO:USDC ) usually maintain a value close to $1. However, these transactions still count as disposals, and the IRS requires taxpayers to keep detailed records of every sale, exchange, or disposal of virtual currency and its fair market value. Mesh and Visa’s new setup benefits individuals who hold stablecoins, receive payments in them, or frequently make cross-border transactions and prefer to spend directly without cashing out first. Stablecoins simplify tax tracking and suit everyday purchases. However, long-term crypto holders may find it more advantageous to keep their investments separate and use a traditional card for payments. Tax tracking is the cost. Each purchase with a coin that has risen in value may create a gain to report. Small purchases add up fast over a year, so frequent spenders of appreciated coins will likely require tax software. If Mesh and its partners publish clear coin and fee lists at launch, this could become one of the easiest ways to spend crypto—as long as users know the tax owed on each transaction. extraction.body: Visa has partnered with crypto payments infrastructure provider Mesh to let consumers spend cryptocurrency and stablecoin balances at more than 175 million merchant locations worldwide without first transferring funds to a bank account or loading a separate payment card. Visa has partnered with Mesh to enable crypto and stablecoin spending at more than 175 million merchant locations across over 200 countries and territories. Consumers will be able to pay directly from supported wallet balances without cashing out, transferring funds or obtaining separate payment cards. Mesh will handle transaction funding and conversion, while merchants continue receiving payments through Visa's existing infrastructure. Participating platforms can offer the service through a single Mesh integration, with the company managing onboarding and customer verification. Initial availability, supported devices and participating crypto wallets have yet to be announced. 19 announcement, Mesh said the partnership would connect digital wallets and cryptocurrency platforms to Visa's payment network through its transaction processing infrastructure, allowing users to make purchases directly from their existing balances. The proposed service will support payments at physical stores and online merchants across more than 200 countries and territories where Visa operates. Mesh will handle the conversion and movement of funds behind each transaction, while merchants receive payments through their existing checkout systems. Visa processed $14.2 trillion in payment volume during fiscal 2025, according to figures cited in the announcement. Visa and Mesh will connect crypto wallets to existing payment terminals Under the agreement, Mesh will allow participating wallet providers and cryptocurrency platforms to offer payments directly from digital asset balances without requiring customers to withdraw their holdings before making a purchase. The payment process will rely on a Visa credential created in the background. Mesh will manage the funding and conversion process when a transaction takes place, drawing from supported cryptocurrency, stablecoin or fiat balances. Merchants will continue receiving payments through Visa's existing infrastructure, without installing new hardware or changing how they accept transactions. The arrangement does not mean merchants will receive cryptocurrency directly. Mesh will handle the conversion required to complete payments through the conventional payment network. According to the company, wallet providers can activate the service through a single Mesh integration without developing and operating their own card programs. Mesh will act as the program manager and handle customer onboarding and know your customer checks associated with the service. The company said its network already serves more than 200 enterprises and connects hundreds of wallets, exchanges and financial platforms. Its existing enterprise relationships include Kalshi, Tools for Humanity, Félix Pago, Majority and KAST, although the announcement did not confirm which partners would participate in the initial Visa rollout. "Crypto never had a spending problem, it has a last-mile problem," Mesh co-founder and CEO Bam Azizi said in the announcement. Azizi said the company's infrastructure would manage funding and conversion at the time of payment, removing the need for customers to move money between accounts before making purchases. Visa's global head of growth, Rubail Birwadker, said the collaboration would give consumers more ways to use digital asset balances through established payment services. Visa expands stablecoin payments beyond dedicated card programs The partnership follows several initiatives by Visa to connect cryptocurrency holdings and stablecoin transactions with its existing payments infrastructure. In September, Visa disclosed that more than 160 stablecoin card programs were operating globally during its fiscal second quarter of 2026. Payment volume across those programs had climbed nearly 200% from the previous year, while the company's stablecoin settlement business surpassed an annualized rate of $20 billion. An October update showed that stablecoin card payments continued to record nearly 200% annual growth across Visa's network. Business and commercial programs accounted for approximately 17% of the company's stablecoin-linked card payment volume during fiscal 2026. The Mesh arrangement uses a different customer-facing model from conventional cryptocurrency card programs because participating platforms can provide payment access without requiring customers to obtain a separate card associated with each wallet. Earlier payment integrations have generally required users to convert cryptocurrency into fiat before spending it or rely on dedicated cards issued through specific providers. In January, Visa partnered with Mercuryo to allow eligible users to convert cryptocurrency into fiat and transfer the proceeds to Visa debit and credit cards through Visa Direct. The service was designed to deliver funds to eligible cards within minutes, depending on the supported market and payment conditions. Visa entered another digital asset agreement in October when it partnered with ADI Foundation to explore blockchain infrastructure and digital payment systems. That agreement remained exploratory, with neither company announcing a specific blockchain, stablecoin or commercial launch date. Mesh builds on existing exchange and stablecoin integrations Mesh has spent much of 2026 adding cryptocurrency exchanges, wallets and payment platforms to its network. In September, crypto.news reported that Bybit Pay integrated Mesh to connect its payment service with more than 300 wallets, exchanges and financial platforms.

As a result, spending crypto is a taxable event, similar to selling it. The IRS states that “an exchange of digital assets for property, goods, or services” constitutes a taxable transaction. According to Form 1040 instructions, you must report any disposal through payment on Form 8949 and Schedule D. For instance, if someone purchases a $1,000 laptop using Bitcoin bought at $500, they owe taxes on the $500 gain , even if they haven’t converted any crypto to cash. At the 15% long-term capital gains rate (for assets held over a year), the laptop adds about $75 to their tax bill. Coins held for a year or less are taxed at the regular income tax rate, which is usually higher. Additionally, a purchase can lock in a loss. For example, if Bitcoin trades at about $81,000 , down from $111,000 a year earlier, selling coins bought at the higher price would realize a capital loss that could offset other capital gains. Stablecoins largely avoid these complexities, as tokens like USD Coin ( CRYPTO:USDC ) usually maintain a value close to $1. Mesh and Visa ( NYSE:V | V Price Prediction ) have teamed up to let users spend crypto and stablecoin balances held in wallet apps at more than 175 million merchants worldwide, without needing a separate crypto card. The company announced this significant development on October 19, 2026.

Many crypto holders have never spent their digital assets in stores. Until now, converting crypto to cash often required selling coins, waiting for the funds to transfer to a bank, or signing up for a crypto debit card linked to a specific exchange.
While the checkout process is straightforward under this new arrangement, tax considerations can catch new users off guard. Here’s what to expect at checkout and what tax implications may follow.

The wallet app takes care of most of the payment process. According to the announcement, the participating wallet app sets up a Visa card behind the scenes. Users can tap a standard contactless terminal or check out online without selling, transferring, or preloading any funds.

When it’s time to pay, Mesh determines how the purchase is funded—crypto, a stablecoin (a token designed to maintain a steady $1 value), or regular dollars. The merchant receives the payment as a standard Visa transaction, requiring no additional hardware and ensuring cashiers see a typical card payment.
"Fishpool gold coins" by Lawrence OP is licensed under BY 2.0.

Mesh has not yet specified which cryptocurrencies it will support, any applicable fees, or which countries it will include in the initial rollout. Users should check their wallet apps to confirm three critical details before buying.

The IRS classifies cryptocurrencies as property. As a result, spending crypto is a taxable event, similar to selling it. The IRS states that “an exchange of digital assets for property, goods, or services” constitutes a taxable transaction. According to Form 1040 instructions, you must report any disposal through payment on Form 8949 and Schedule D.

For instance, if someone purchases a $1,000 laptop using Bitcoin bought at $500, they owe taxes on the $500 gain , even if they haven’t converted any crypto to cash. At the 15% long-term capital gains rate (for assets held over a year), the laptop adds about $75 to their tax bill. Coins held for a year or less are taxed at the regular income tax rate, which is usually higher.

Additionally, a purchase can lock in a loss. For example, if Bitcoin trades at about $81,000 , down from $111,000 a year earlier, selling coins bought at the higher price would realize a capital loss that could offset other capital gains.

Stablecoins largely avoid these complexities, as tokens like USD Coin ( CRYPTO:USDC ) usually maintain a value close to $1. However, these transactions still count as disposals, and the IRS requires taxpayers to keep detailed records of every sale, exchange, or disposal of virtual currency and its fair market value.

Mesh and Visa’s new setup benefits individuals who hold stablecoins, receive payments in them, or frequently make cross-border transactions and prefer to spend directly without cashing out first. Stablecoins simplify tax tracking and suit everyday purchases. However, long-term crypto holders may find it more advantageous to keep their investments separate and use a traditional card for payments.

Tax tracking is the cost. Each purchase with a coin that has risen in value may create a gain to report. Small purchases add up fast over a year, so frequent spenders of appreciated coins will likely require tax software. If Mesh and its partners publish clear coin and fee lists at launch, this could become one of the easiest ways to spend crypto—as long as users know the tax owed on each transaction.
