extraction.body: Apple will announce a second wave of new products on Wednesday, October 28. Like the October 13 "Welcome Home" announcement, "Pro and Tell" isn't going to be a traditional Apple event, but some members of the media have been invited to Los Angeles to get hands-on time with the new devices. Everyone not invited to Los Angeles will get to see the product announcements via press releases that come out on October 28. Apple could send out press releases at 10:00 a.m. Pacific Time, which is when the media experience will begin. Press release announcements typically come out earlier in the morning around 9:00 a.m. Eastern Time, so that's also a possibility. The "Pro and Tell" name gives us a strong hint at what's coming: the MacBook Pro . It will be joined by other new Macs and a new iPad . New high-end ‌MacBook Pro‌ models are coming with two firsts for the Mac line: OLED display technology and a touchscreen. Design changes are expected too, but the new ‌MacBook Pro‌ models are going to use the same chips as the current version. Apple might keep selling the current ‌MacBook Pro‌ models and add the ‌OLED‌ models as a higher-end, more expensive option. While there were rumors suggesting the ‌OLED‌ MacBook would be called the MacBook Ultra , it's now clear Apple is sticking with Pro. ‌OLED‌ displays are expensive, and touch modules also add cost, so the ‌OLED‌ ‌MacBook Pro‌ models will likely cost more than the current ‌MacBook Pro‌ models. The 14-inch entry-level ‌MacBook Pro‌ is expected to get an M6 chip to replace the M5 chip it was updated with in October 2025. No other design changes are expected. Rumors suggest Apple will update the 24-inch iMac with an M6 chip too. As with the entry-level ‌MacBook Pro‌, it won't get external changes. Along with the new Macs that are coming, we're expecting an iPad mini update. The ‌iPad mini‌ 8 is going to get an ‌OLED‌ display, making it the first ‌iPad‌ other than the iPad Pro to adopt ‌OLED‌. It's also going to get a design refresh with a vibration-based speaker setup that eliminates speaker holes and allows for a more water-resistant design. It could be the first ‌iPad‌ with an IP rating, able to hold up to splashes and possibly even submersion. The ‌iPad mini‌ 8 is expected to use the same A20 Pro chip that's in the iPhone 18 Pro models. It's so far unclear whether the ‌iPad mini‌ will continue to have a 60Hz refresh rate or if it will get a 120Hz ProMotion upgrade. The front camera will relocated from the portrait side to the landscape side, a change Apple previously made in other ‌iPad‌ models. Waterproofing and ‌OLED‌ are expected to push up the price, so the new model could cost around $200 more than the current $599 model. extraction.body: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station. Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money. That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. Rise of cryptocurrency crimes, and how kiosks can play a role Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. States are upping regulations, oversight over crypto ATMs. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Jackson Some of the bill's language includes: Requiring licenses for all kiosk operators under the Money Transmissions Act. It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. You don't have to do that through a gas station. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. We have advocated for a waiting period for first-time customers because it gives time to stop a scam before any funds leave. CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state.

extraction.body: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station. Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money. That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. The transactions are virtually instant, difficult to trace and can be difficult to reverse. Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Neal Jackson (R). "HB920 aims to protect North Carolinians from fraud through appropriate regulatory oversight while preserving our citizens ability to manage their finances. As technology advances, this legislation embraces innovation while ensuring consumers have the protections they deserve," says Rep. Jackson It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. In an effort to reduce fraud, the bill also seeks to place limitations on transaction amounts, capping new customers at $2,000 daily for the first 30 days, and after that, at $5,000. North Carolina Attorney General Jeff Jackson believes the new customer limit may be the bill's most significant addition to protecting consumers. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. "We don't think there is any legitimate use for these devices. They are overwhelmingly used for fraud. If you want to invest in Bitcoin, you can do that without paying the 12% overhead. You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. David Tente, the executive director of the ATM Industry Association, pushed back on Attorney General Jackson's assessment of how frequently the kiosks are used to facilitate crimes. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. "Many of the [bill] requirements are similar to the bill Congress is working on. However, the 30-day return requirement makes everything else rather pointless. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Rep. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. Longest said. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Answers to questions are published in full for accuracy. Question: Which HB 920 changes will require you to update your kiosks? Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. The changes we are implementing before January 1, 2027 include: CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. CoinFlip has held a North Carolina money transmitter license since May 2024 and supports clear, consistent rules and accountability for all operators. We will implement the changes necessary to comply with the law’s requirements for when they take effect. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? Byte Federal: Complying with NC regulation is an easy lift for Byte Federal because we already meet the same standards in other states. The problem is the 12% fee cap, a regulation that puts legitimate operators running full compliance out of business in NC. We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state. CoinFlip: CoinFlip currently operates 152 kiosks across the state and has no plans to reduce its North Carolina kiosk network as a result of the new law.” Question: What is your policy for refunding scam victims? Byte Federal: We will comply fully with HB 920's refund provisions. Under the law, when the Commissioner of Banks determines a transaction was fraudulent and the victim reported it within 30 days, new customers receive a full refund and existing customers receive a refund of fees. That said, we believe the refund mandate holds compliant kiosk operators to a standard no other part of the financial system is held to. Byte Federal operates under the same federal framework as banks and other money transmitters: the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act's customer identification and due diligence rules, OFAC sanctions screening, and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's privacy and data-security requirements. Yet when a bank customer is tricked into sending a wire to a scammer, the bank generally does not refund that loss. Federal consumer protection rules for electronic transfers do not cover wire transfers. Wires instead fall under Article 4A of the Uniform Commercial Code, which relieves a bank of any refund obligation when it processed the customer's payment in good faith and followed agreed security procedures. Courts have applied this to scam victims directly. In one 2024 federal case, a customer who wired money to fraudulent crypto companies could not recover it from the bank, because the customer had authorized the wires and the bank had followed its procedures. A bitcoin transaction is just as irreversible as a wire. When a customer has passed identity verification, read our scam warnings, completed a verification call if they are 60 or older, and attested that they are sending funds to their own wallet without anyone directing them, we do not believe a compliant operator should be treated differently from a bank. The money in a kiosk is not the operators to give back, and the person responsible for the loss is the criminal who stole it. More broadly, we believe the most effective protection is stopping a scam before any money is sent. Once bitcoin is sent, it cannot be recalled by us or anyone else. That is why our program focuses on the moments before a transaction: the 60+ verification calls, attestations, wallet screening, and now the 48-hour new-customer hold, during which funds can still be returned. Outside the framework established by state law, we provide refunds where Byte Federal failed to follow its required compliance procedures. We also cooperate with law enforcement on every fraud report and provide transaction and wallet data to help trace and recover funds. CoinFlip: Our current policy provides transaction-fee refunds to confirmed scam victims. Identifying and stopping suspected scams before funds are transferred is critical when we hold a transaction before a transfer is complete; we can return it to the principal. Refund requests and reported scams are evaluated case by case, and our live support team helps customers report scams and request refunds. When a scam is reported, CoinFlip works with law enforcement to help stop or track scammers. Because blockchain transactions create a public record, investigators may be able to trace funds and, in some cases, assist with recovery. CoinFlip also blocks suspicious transactions and permanently blacklists high-risk digital wallet addresses, so they cannot be used at a CoinFlip kiosk again. We will honor the additional refund rights established by North Carolina’s new law when it takes effect.”

extraction.body: In seconds, her financial security vanished behind a screen inside a gas station. Thousands of dollars deposited into a cryptocurrency ATM, in what one Johnston County woman thought was a payment to law enforcement for her safe release. But when the callers – impersonating local law enforcement – on the other end of the line requested an additional $4,000, she told them she simply didn’t have the money. That’s when the call dropped, and she realized she had been depleted of what she says was the entirety of her savings. “I just set up an appointment with a counselor, so I'd have somebody to talk to, because it's really hurt me financially and hurt me mentally." This victim, who wished to share her story with WRAL but not to be identified, is among thousands of victims across the country taken advantage of via a cryptocurrency kiosk. Public records out of Harnett County show a man recently lost more than $30,000 – which was described as 'almost all' of his savings – to a cryptocurrency machine. The machines – which upon first glance resemble regular ATMs – convert deposited cash into cryptocurrency investments. Rise of cryptocurrency crimes, and how kiosks can play a role Internet crimes facilitated through cryptocurrency kiosks are rising, following similar trends with general cryptocurrency related crimes. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) began publicly reporting cryptocurrency kiosk metrics as of 2023. That year, the FBI received 5,500 complaints related to cryptocurrency kiosks, with losses of more than $189 million. Those numbers jumped in 2025, with the agency reporting 13,460 complaints totaling $389 million in victim losses. "Fraud losses at BTMs [Bitcoin ATMs] are skyrocketing, increasing nearly tenfold from 2020 to 2023," according to data cited from the Federal Trade Commission's (FTC) Consumer Sentinel Network. States are upping regulations, oversight over crypto ATMs. Many states are enacting tighter consumer regulations around cryptocurrency kiosks, including several who have imposed some kind of ban altogether. This year, North Carolina state lawmakers approved several regulatory changes to the Bitcoin ATM (BTM) industry by passing House Bill 920, introduced by State Rep. Jackson Some of the bill's language includes: Requiring licenses for all kiosk operators under the Money Transmissions Act. It stipulates that kiosk operators shall refund the "full dollar amount deposited" under certain conditions, including when someone reports a "fraudulent" transmission within 30 days. Although the bill's changes go into effect in 2027, Jackson questions – based on the level of fraud cases he's seen from this technology – if there is a legitimate reason to have any in the state in the first place. You don't have to do that through a gas station. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. "Only a tiny percentage of those transactions are fraud," Tente told WRAL via email. Crypto deployers are highly unlikely to operate under such rules." State Rep. Tim Longest, D-Wake, previously expressed concern to WRAL about having the kiosks at all in the state. Longest, a consumer protection lawyer, said the bill's protections could have been stronger. "I think that we should really question whether these regulations go far enough and if these machines really serve any legitimate purpose," Rep. "You don't go to put cash in a machine and take out a stock, and yet a stock is exactly the same kind of speculative asset that cryptocurrency is." Attorney General Jackson alluded to the DOJ currently looking into cryptocurrency kiosk companies. "Investigation underway as we speak," Jackson said. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. We have advocated for a waiting period for first-time customers because it gives time to stop a scam before any funds leave. CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state.

You don't have to do that through a gas station. If you want to send money to somebody, you can do that through a bank. There is no reason to go to one of these machines," he told WRAL. WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws. Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies. Answers to questions are published in full for accuracy. Question: Which HB 920 changes will require you to update your kiosks? Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. The changes we are implementing before January 1, 2027 include: CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. CoinFlip has held a North Carolina money transmitter license since May 2024 and supports clear, consistent rules and accountability for all operators. We will implement the changes necessary to comply with the law’s requirements for when they take effect. Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks? Byte Federal: Complying with NC regulation is an easy lift for Byte Federal because we already meet the same standards in other states. The problem is the 12% fee cap, a regulation that puts legitimate operators running full compliance out of business in NC. We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state. CoinFlip: CoinFlip currently operates 152 kiosks across the state and has no plans to reduce its North Carolina kiosk network as a result of the new law.” Question: What is your policy for refunding scam victims? Byte Federal: We will comply fully with HB 920's refund provisions. Under the law, when the Commissioner of Banks determines a transaction was fraudulent and the victim reported it within 30 days, new customers receive a full refund and existing customers receive a refund of fees. That said, we believe the refund mandate holds compliant kiosk operators to a standard no other part of the financial system is held to. Byte Federal operates under the same federal framework as banks and other money transmitters: the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act's customer identification and due diligence rules, OFAC sanctions screening, and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's privacy and data-security requirements. Yet when a bank customer is tricked into sending a wire to a scammer, the bank generally does not refund that loss. Federal consumer protection rules for electronic transfers do not cover wire transfers. Wires instead fall under Article 4A of the Uniform Commercial Code, which relieves a bank of any refund obligation when it processed the customer's payment in good faith and followed agreed security procedures. Courts have applied this to scam victims directly. In one 2024 federal case, a customer who wired money to fraudulent crypto companies could not recover it from the bank, because the customer had authorized the wires and the bank had followed its procedures. A bitcoin transaction is just as irreversible as a wire. When a customer has passed identity verification, read our scam warnings, completed a verification call if they are 60 or older, and attested that they are sending funds to their own wallet without anyone directing them, we do not believe a compliant operator should be treated differently from a bank. The money in a kiosk is not the operators to give back, and the person responsible for the loss is the criminal who stole it. More broadly, we believe the most effective protection is stopping a scam before any money is sent. Once bitcoin is sent, it cannot be recalled by us or anyone else. That is why our program focuses on the moments before a transaction: the 60+ verification calls, attestations, wallet screening, and now the 48-hour new-customer hold, during which funds can still be returned. Outside the framework established by state law, we provide refunds where Byte Federal failed to follow its required compliance procedures. We also cooperate with law enforcement on every fraud report and provide transaction and wallet data to help trace and recover funds. CoinFlip: Our current policy provides transaction-fee refunds to confirmed scam victims. Identifying and stopping suspected scams before funds are transferred is critical when we hold a transaction before a transfer is complete; we can return it to the principal. Refund requests and reported scams are evaluated case by case, and our live support team helps customers report scams and request refunds. When a scam is reported, CoinFlip works with law enforcement to help stop or track scammers. Because blockchain transactions create a public record, investigators may be able to trace funds and, in some cases, assist with recovery. CoinFlip also blocks suspicious transactions and permanently blacklists high-risk digital wallet addresses, so they cannot be used at a CoinFlip kiosk again. We will honor the additional refund rights established by North Carolina’s new law when it takes effect.”

WRAL reached out to several cryptocurrency kiosk companies operating in North Carolina, requesting information on how they plan to comply with new state laws.

Below are responses from Byte Federal, through founder and chief compliance officer Mark Paolillo, and Chief Executive Officer, Paul Tarantino, as well as a marketing spokesperson for CoinFlip. They say many of the protections are already in place, independently, as part of their company's policies.
Answers to questions are published in full for accuracy.
Question: Which HB 920 changes will require you to update your kiosks?

Byte Federal: Most of HB 920's requirements match what we already do: scam warnings, blockchain analytics, live customer service, a written anti-fraud program, and dedicated compliance staff. The changes we are implementing before January 1, 2027 include:

CoinFlip: CoinFlip already provides many of the consumer protections required under North Carolina’s new cryptocurrency kiosk law, including live customer support, scam warnings, and technology that screens for suspicious digital wallets. We appreciate the leadership of Representative Jackson and the collaborative efforts of stakeholders in developing a regulatory framework that strengthens consumer protections while preserving access to legitimate financial services. CoinFlip has held a North Carolina money transmitter license since May 2024 and supports clear, consistent rules and accountability for all operators. We will implement the changes necessary to comply with the law’s requirements for when they take effect.
Question: Does the company plan to reduce its number of North Carolina kiosks?

Byte Federal: Complying with NC regulation is an easy lift for Byte Federal because we already meet the same standards in other states. The problem is the 12% fee cap, a regulation that puts legitimate operators running full compliance out of business in NC. We are optimistic that NC lawmakers can see the error in the fee cap and make adjustments that allow legitimate kiosk operators to do business in the state.
CoinFlip: CoinFlip currently operates 152 kiosks across the state and has no plans to reduce its North Carolina kiosk network as a result of the new law.”
Question: What is your policy for refunding scam victims?

Byte Federal: We will comply fully with HB 920's refund provisions. Under the law, when the Commissioner of Banks determines a transaction was fraudulent and the victim reported it within 30 days, new customers receive a full refund and existing customers receive a refund of fees.

That said, we believe the refund mandate holds compliant kiosk operators to a standard no other part of the financial system is held to. Byte Federal operates under the same federal framework as banks and other money transmitters: the Bank Secrecy Act, the USA PATRIOT Act's customer identification and due diligence rules, OFAC sanctions screening, and the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's privacy and data-security requirements. Yet when a bank customer is tricked into sending a wire to a scammer, the bank generally does not refund that loss. Federal consumer protection rules for electronic transfers do not cover wire transfers. Wires instead fall under Article 4A of the Uniform Commercial Code, which relieves a bank of any refund obligation when it processed the customer's payment in good faith and followed agreed security procedures. Courts have applied this to scam victims directly. In one 2024 federal case, a customer who wired money to fraudulent crypto companies could not recover it from the bank, because the customer had authorized the wires and the bank had followed its procedures. A bitcoin transaction is just as irreversible as a wire. When a customer has passed identity verification, read our scam warnings, completed a verification call if they are 60 or older, and attested that they are sending funds to their own wallet without anyone directing them, we do not believe a compliant operator should be treated differently from a bank. The money in a kiosk is not the operators to give back, and the person responsible for the loss is the criminal who stole it.

More broadly, we believe the most effective protection is stopping a scam before any money is sent. Once bitcoin is sent, it cannot be recalled by us or anyone else. That is why our program focuses on the moments before a transaction: the 60+ verification calls, attestations, wallet screening, and now the 48-hour new-customer hold, during which funds can still be returned. Outside the framework established by state law, we provide refunds where Byte Federal failed to follow its required compliance procedures. We also cooperate with law enforcement on every fraud report and provide transaction and wallet data to help trace and recover funds.

CoinFlip: Our current policy provides transaction-fee refunds to confirmed scam victims. Identifying and stopping suspected scams before funds are transferred is critical when we hold a transaction before a transfer is complete; we can return it to the principal. Refund requests and reported scams are evaluated case by case, and our live support team helps customers report scams and request refunds. When a scam is reported, CoinFlip works with law enforcement to help stop or track scammers. Because blockchain transactions create a public record, investigators may be able to trace funds and, in some cases, assist with recovery. CoinFlip also blocks suspicious transactions and permanently blacklists high-risk digital wallet addresses, so they cannot be used at a CoinFlip kiosk again. We will honor the additional refund rights established by North Carolina’s new law when it takes effect.”

The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution has produced two of the fastest-growing start-ups in history. OpenAI burst onto the scene in late 2022 when it launched ChatGPT, introducing consumers around the world to generative AI. Meanwhile, Anthropic has emerged as a formidable competitor with its Claude models. Both companies' growth has been extraordinary. Following a $122 billion funding round in March, OpenAI reached a valuation of $852 billion, while Anthropic was valued at $965 billion after its Series H round in May. Naturally, AI investors are eager to know when they can buy shares. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Anthropic confidentially filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in June and could make its public debut as soon as next month. OpenAI has also explored going public, although its timing remains uncertain. Here's an interesting alternative: Rather than waiting for either company to go public at a valuation approaching the trillion-dollar milestone, investors can buy Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) instead. Alphabet stands to benefit regardless of which AI developer ultimately wins. Read on to learn why. One of Alphabet's quiet advantages is that it doesn't need its Gemini AI models to beat ChatGPT or Claude. That reason is Google Cloud provides compute infrastructure to its competitors. In May 2025, OpenAI agreed to use Google Cloud's capacity to train and deploy its AI models. This relationship is particularly interesting because up to that point, OpenAI was primarily tied to Microsoft Azure. Adding Google provided OpenAI with an alternative source of AI compute while giving Alphabet a hyperscaler customer whose infrastructure requirements are enormous. Anthropic's relationship with Google runs even deeper. In October 2025, Anthropic announced its use of Google's custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). In April, this relationship was expanded to include multiple gigawatts of TPU capacity expected to come online in 2027. These arrangements create an attractive business model for Alphabet because the company can develop AI products for consumers while simultaneously supplying infrastructure that competing enterprises need. The strategy is already producing impressive results. During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. While not all of that growth came from OpenAI and Anthropic, their expanding infrastructure commitments underscore why Google Cloud should remain a major beneficiary of the AI boom. Alphabet isn't just an infrastructure partner to Anthropic. It's also one of the company's largest investors. Google initially invested in Anthropic in 2023. But by early 2026, Alphabet had invested roughly $3 billion in Anthropic and owned an estimated 14% equity stake. In April, Google announced plans to invest up to another $40 billion. The deal was structured to include an initial $10 billion commitment, with an additional $30 billion contingent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. Why is Google investing so heavily in a company whose generative models compete directly with Gemini? The answer is simple: Alphabet is positioned to benefit from Anthropic's success in multiple ways. First, its equity investment will appreciate as Anthropic's valuation increases. Additionally, Anthropic is a major customer for Google's cloud infrastructure and custom AI chips. Third, Google's tie-up with Anthropic gives it exposure to an alternative AI ecosystem, reducing its dependence on Gemini emerging as the industry's go-to model. This is an unusually versatile position to be in. If Anthropic goes public at its reported $2 trillion valuation, a hypothetical 14% stake would be worth $280 billion. This shows how Alphabet can participate in one of the largest IPOs in history without investors needing to lift a finger and buy Anthropic stock directly. OpenAI's valuation of $852 billion represents approximately 17 times its reported $50 billion annualized revenue run rate. Meanwhile, Anthropic's $965 billion valuation represents 14 times its Q3 annualized revenue run rate of $67.2 billion. At a $2 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would trade at nearly 30 times its current revenue run rate. These are enormous premiums, especially considering the capital expenditures required to develop advanced AI. Moreover, OpenAI remains unprofitable while Anthropic recently reported a small profit on an adjusted operating basis. Alphabet offers a much different financial profile. During Q2, the company generated $120 billion in revenue and roughly $40.8 billion in operating income. Alphabet stock trades around a 23 times forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio -- a relatively reasonable valuation considering its established and highly profitable advertising and cloud businesses. While OpenAI and Anthropic could become respected public companies, their anticipated valuations already reflect high expectations. Alphabet offers investors exposure to both AI developers through Google Cloud, an existing equity stake in Anthropic, and its own growing AI ecosystem. Combined with its AI-driven revenue and robust profitability, I see Alphabet as the more compelling AI stock to buy and hold ahead of these anticipated mega-IPOs. Before you buy stock in Alphabet, consider this: The Motley Fool Stock Advisor analyst team just identified what they believe are the 10 best stocks for investors to buy now… and Alphabet wasn't one of them. The 10 stocks that made the cut could produce monster returns in the coming years. Consider when Netflix made this list on December 17, 2004... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $380,363 !* Or when Nvidia made this list on April 15, 2005... if you invested $1,000 at the time of our recommendation, you'd have $1,315,732 !* Now, it's worth noting Stock Advisor's total average return is 919% — a market-crushing outperformance compared to 211% for the S&P 500. The strategy is already producing impressive results. During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. While not all of that growth came from OpenAI and Anthropic, their expanding infrastructure commitments underscore why Google Cloud should remain a major beneficiary of the AI boom.

Alphabet isn't just an infrastructure partner to Anthropic. It's also one of the company's largest investors. Google initially invested in Anthropic in 2023. But by early 2026, Alphabet had invested roughly $3 billion in Anthropic and owned an estimated 14% equity stake. In April, Google announced plans to invest up to another $40 billion. The deal was structured to include an initial $10 billion commitment, with an additional $30 billion contingent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones.
Why is Google investing so heavily in a company whose generative models compete directly with Gemini?

The answer is simple: Alphabet is positioned to benefit from Anthropic's success in multiple ways. First, its equity investment will appreciate as Anthropic's valuation increases. Additionally, Anthropic is a major customer for Google's cloud infrastructure and custom AI chips. Third, Google's tie-up with Anthropic gives it exposure to an alternative AI ecosystem, reducing its dependence on Gemini emerging as the industry's go-to model.

This is an unusually versatile position to be in. If Anthropic goes public at its reported $2 trillion valuation, a hypothetical 14% stake would be worth $280 billion. This shows how Alphabet can participate in one of the largest IPOs in history without investors needing to lift a finger and buy Anthropic stock directly.

OpenAI's valuation of $852 billion represents approximately 17 times its reported $50 billion annualized revenue run rate. Meanwhile, Anthropic's $965 billion valuation represents 14 times its Q3 annualized revenue run rate of $67.2 billion. At a $2 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would trade at nearly 30 times its current revenue run rate.

These are enormous premiums, especially considering the capital expenditures required to develop advanced AI. Moreover, OpenAI remains unprofitable while Anthropic recently reported a small profit on an adjusted operating basis.

Alphabet offers a much different financial profile. During Q2, the company generated $120 billion in revenue and roughly $40.8 billion in operating income. Alphabet stock trades around a 23 times forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio -- a relatively reasonable valuation considering its established and highly profitable advertising and cloud businesses.

While OpenAI and Anthropic could become respected public companies, their anticipated valuations already reflect high expectations. Alphabet offers investors exposure to both AI developers through Google Cloud, an existing equity stake in Anthropic, and its own growing AI ecosystem. Combined with its AI-driven revenue and robust profitability, I see Alphabet as the more compelling AI stock to buy and hold ahead of these anticipated mega-IPOs.

Russell Thompson, the Chief Investment Officer at Hilbert Group, turned short-term bearish on Bitcoin on October 9 and reiterated his stance in his weekly report. Nonetheless, he remains optimistic about Bitcoin’s medium-term outlook, suggesting it may be a good opportunity to buy during dips.
Bitcoin has lost its 50-day average four times in 2026.

The worst drop came after the May break, when Bitcoin fell from $75,444 to $59,073, a 21.7% decline. However, the declines following the July and August breaks were much milder, with drops of 2.4% and 0.5%, respectively, before Bitcoin rebounded to close at $77,054 on August 22.
With four instances of breaking the 50-day average this year, it’s hard to predict outcomes from such a small sample.

Over the past month, Bitcoin gained 0.4%, while Ethereum ( CRYPTO:ETH ) fell 9.5%, Solana ( CRYPTO:SOL ) dropped 6%, and XRP ( CRYPTO:XRP ) lost 8.1%. Over the past year, Bitcoin remains ahead, down 26.3%, compared to Ethereum’s 39.9%, Solana’s 44.9%, and XRP’s 48.1% decline.

Bitcoin’s market dominance currently stands at 59.6%. When investor sentiment turns cautious, money typically flows out of smaller cryptocurrencies and into Bitcoin, which benefits from deeper trading markets and steady demand from spot ETFs. This trend likely explains why Bitcoin has held above its 50-day average longer than other major coins.

Trading activity has also decreased, with total crypto trading volume down by 1.5% in the last 24 hours. Bitcoin’s most active trading session recently occurred on September 21, when the price rose from a close of $81,160 the previous day to $86,595. When Bitcoin declines on low trading volume, it signals calm among sellers, but buyers appear hesitant.

Hilbert identifies several crucial support levels for Bitcoin: the immediate 50-day average at $81,538, followed by $79,000, which represents the max pain level as options expiry approaches. The “max pain” level is the price point at which the most options contracts expire worthless, causing the biggest losses for option buyers. Prices sometimes gravitate toward this level as expiry nears, with BTC touching $79,676 on October 15.

Below that, Thompson notes trend-line support at $77,000, and Hilbert mentions a moving-average support band that extends down to $72,000. Even $72,000 is considerably higher than the $59,073 low from June 5.

Options traders appear to be adopting a defensive approach. According to Hilbert, put options—contracts that gain value when prices drop—trade at a 16-point premium over call options, which gain value when prices rise. Additionally, implied volatility, which estimates potential price swings, is 35, above the realized volatility of 32.5, suggesting traders are pricing in more volatility than the market has delivered recently.

We believe Bitcoin is likely to close below its 50-day average soon; however, the support levels beneath it appear stronger than they did in May. A drop below this average alone wouldn’t be a strong signal, especially given the mixed signals we’ve seen from Bitcoin’s movements in 2026.
A daily close below $77,000 would be a more concerning indicator, as it would break Hilbert’s trend line and bring the $72,000 support level into focus.

On the upside, Hilbert suggests that if Bitcoin breaks and holds above $88,000, it could pave the way for prices in the mid-$90,000s. Bitcoin’s recent high was $87,397 on September 21, just short of that crucial level. Thompson’s medium-term outlook depends on this breakout, accompanied by a surge in inflows like those seen on October 19. A daily close above $88,000 would contradict the current short-term bearish outlook.

passages: Major UK banks are blocking or restricting customers' transfers to crypto platforms, with more than 10,000 complaints filed over a three-month period.
Banks that impose transfer limits received 6,198 complaints, while those without a published policy restricting crypto transfers received 2,842.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Lloyds Banking Group (LON: LLOY) received the most complaints, at 2,297, followed by Barclays (LON: BARC) with 1,569 and NatWest Group (LON: NWG) with 1,278.
Lloyds, which includes Halifax and Bank of Scotland, accounted for more than 22% of the total complaints.
The complaints involved all major UK retail banks and came from every one of the country's 650 parliamentary constituencies.
HSBC UK (LSE: HSBA) and Monzo were also among the banks named in the report, which found that restrictions were not limited to institutions with explicit crypto bans.

Stand With Crypto said the figures suggest customers cannot reliably predict whether their bank will allow them to transfer money to regulated crypto platforms, even when the bank does not publicly prohibit such payments.

sources.title: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys - Decrypt
passages: Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards.

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.”

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”
Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

extraction.body: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards. Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.” The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections. Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit. Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.” The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022. Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 . In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account. Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card. This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money. “If Barclaycard doesn't want to lend money to crypto traders, that's up to them,” he said. “They need to manage their own risk as they see fit, and they make a good point that crypto losses are never covered by the financial services compensation scheme.” However, Goodman added that it really “annoys” him when UK banks refuse to let people send their own money from their own bank account to a crypto trading account. “And that happens more often than you might think," he adds. Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively. Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved. Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.”

The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections.
Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.
Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 .
In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account.
Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

“If Barclaycard doesn't want to lend money to crypto traders, that's up to them,” he said. “They need to manage their own risk as they see fit, and they make a good point that crypto losses are never covered by the financial services compensation scheme.”
However, Goodman added that it really “annoys” him when UK banks refuse to let people send their own money from their own bank account to a crypto trading account.
“And that happens more often than you might think," he adds.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.
Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved.

"Experienced crypto traders often borrow money to trade, just as advanced stock market traders do,” he says. “But it takes skill to manage your risk sensibly and a lot of traders go broke when they get it wrong.”

coreStoryFacts.text: Major UK banks are blocking or restricting customers' transfers to crypto platforms, with more than 10,000 complaints filed over a three-month period.
Banks that impose transfer limits received 6,198 complaints, while those without a published policy restricting crypto transfers received 2,842.
Yahoo Finance is not a broker-dealer or investment adviser and does not offer securities or cryptocurrencies for sale or facilitate trading.
Lloyds Banking Group (LON: LLOY) received the most complaints, at 2,297, followed by Barclays (LON: BARC) with 1,569 and NatWest Group (LON: NWG) with 1,278.
Lloyds, which includes Halifax and Bank of Scotland, accounted for more than 22% of the total complaints.
The complaints involved all major UK retail banks and came from every one of the country's 650 parliamentary constituencies.
HSBC UK (LSE: HSBA) and Monzo were also among the banks named in the report, which found that restrictions were not limited to institutions with explicit crypto bans.

Stand With Crypto said the figures suggest customers cannot reliably predict whether their bank will allow them to transfer money to regulated crypto platforms, even when the bank does not publicly prohibit such payments.

Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.
Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 .
In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account.
Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

“If Barclaycard doesn't want to lend money to crypto traders, that's up to them,” he said. “They need to manage their own risk as they see fit, and they make a good point that crypto losses are never covered by the financial services compensation scheme.”
However, Goodman added that it really “annoys” him when UK banks refuse to let people send their own money from their own bank account to a crypto trading account.
“And that happens more often than you might think," he adds.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.
Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved.

"Experienced crypto traders often borrow money to trade, just as advanced stock market traders do,” he says. “But it takes skill to manage your risk sensibly and a lot of traders go broke when they get it wrong.”

None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds. But Amazon and Google are clearly working to end Nvidia’s advantage.

extraction.body: At the world’s biggest chipmaking complex, Samsung is building the fabs it needs for the AI memory boom. Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes . In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.” Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

sources.title: Gemini can now draw on your Google data to personalize the images it generates - Engadget
passages: Your Google Photos library could soon influence the kind of images you can generate with Gemini.

After letting users personalize the AI assistant's responses with data from Gmail, Search and YouTube, Google says it's bringing that same "Personal Intelligence" to Nano Banana 2 to make it easier for users to create personalized images with the AI model.

Rather than prompting Gemini's image generation model with information about you or photos of your belongings, a direction to "create a picture of my desert island essentials" should produce an image that includes the things you care about without any extra context.

Personalized user data is one of the unique advantages Google has over companies offering competing AI assistants, so expanding Personal Intelligence to an already popular feature like image generation is a natural way to build on that lead.
Google says the feature will come to Gemini in Chrome and other users "soon."

extraction.body: Your Google data can act as an extra reference point for Nano Banana 2. Your Google Photos library could soon influence the kind of images you can generate with Gemini. After letting users personalize the AI assistant's responses with data from Gmail, Search and YouTube, Google says it's bringing that same "Personal Intelligence" to Nano Banana 2 to make it easier for users to create personalized images with the AI model. The goal is to have the data affiliated with your Google account — your YouTube history, emails, Google Photos, etc. — provide context to Nano Banana 2 so you don't have to. Rather than prompting Gemini's image generation model with information about you or photos of your belongings, a direction to "create a picture of my desert island essentials" should produce an image that includes the things you care about without any extra context. Similarly, if you use labels in Google Photos to identify people or pets, you can tell Gemini to "create a hand-drawn illustration of mom," and it should be able to use Google Photo's labels to find the right reference photo and create an image of the right person. If Gemini creates images that don't look right, you can still send a follow-up prompt to refine the result, or select a new source image from Google Photos with the "+" button. Google says you can also click the "Sources" button to view what images the AI referenced in the first place, or ask it directly for the attribution and sources used for a specific image. Personalized user data is one of the unique advantages Google has over companies offering competing AI assistants, so expanding Personal Intelligence to an already popular feature like image generation is a natural way to build on that lead. For now, this more personalized version of Nano Banana 2 is available in the Gemini app for eligible AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. Google says the feature will come to Gemini in Chrome and other users "soon."

sources.title: Google is bringing a more personal version of its Gemini AI assistant to your car
passages: Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products.
Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language.
Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said.

Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in , software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle.
Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto.
That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence.
This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps.

extraction.body: Google is making the Gemini AI assistant that’s already in millions of cars, trucks, and SUVs a lot more personal — a move that could push consumers even deeper into the company’s ecosystem of products. The company said Tuesday it’s upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences. Google said it will roll out “Personal Intelligence with Gemini” to vehicles in two ways — through Android Auto, an app that runs on the user’s phone and wirelessly communicates with and projects navigation, media, and messaging to the vehicle’s infotainment system, and Google Built-in , software and services that have been directly integrated into the vehicle. The feature will launch in Android Auto, starting today, and expand to cars with Google Built-in in the coming months. Google initially launched Gemini last November in Android Auto. Meanwhile, Gemini’s “Personal Intelligence” feature rolled out across the U.S. in March and is now in beta in global markets. This latest upgrade would connect the dots — as Google put it in its blog post — across users’ Google apps. Drivers will have to opt in for Personalized Intelligence to work. Once a user does so, they should expect all sorts of cross-pollination. For instance, a driver who is navigating to the airport may be alerted that the flight on their calendar is delayed. Google said the feature will allow users to make complex requests using natural language. Returning to that airport example, a user might ask the AI assistant for their flight gate before quickly following up with a question about whether it’s still on time. Gemini will give the user answers to both questions at the same time, the company said. That level of emmeshing might make consumers uncomfortable, although Google says users do retain full control over their data with Personal Intelligence. The feature can be turned on or off at any time, and users can selectively choose which apps they’d like to connect, Google said. sources.title: GM Partners with Google to Bring Gemini AI Assistant to Cars in 2026
passages: The Detroit automaker announced Wednesday at its GM Forward event in New York that it's bringing Google's Gemini conversational AI assistant to all its cars, trucks, and SUVs starting in 2026.

The Gemini integration represents the next evolution of GM's existing "Google built-in" platform, which already powers infotainment systems across Buick, Chevrolet, Cadillac, and GMC vehicles with Google Assistant, Maps, and apps.
While the 2026 launch puts GM slightly behind early movers like Tesla and Mercedes, the deep integration with existing Google services and OnStar infrastructure could give it a significant advantage.
According to GM executives at the event, the Gemini-powered assistant will handle far more sophisticated tasks than current voice commands.
For Google, this partnership extends Gemini's reach into the massive automotive market.
The move puts GM squarely in the automotive AI race alongside competitors who've already deployed ChatGPT, Grok, and other conversational assistants in their cars.
Tesla integrated xAI's Grok into its vehicles this summer, Mercedes rolled out ChatGPT integration, and Stellantis partnered with French AI firm Mistral for its own generative assistant.
As cars become increasingly connected and autonomous, the quality of AI assistants could become as important as horsepower or fuel economy in consumer purchasing decisions.

extraction.body: General Motors just announced it's bringing Google's Gemini AI assistant to all its vehicles starting in 2026, marking the automaker's biggest AI integration yet. The move puts GM squarely in the automotive AI race alongside competitors who've already deployed ChatGPT, Grok, and other conversational assistants in their cars. General Motors is diving headfirst into the automotive AI arms race. The Detroit automaker announced Wednesday at its GM Forward event in New York that it's bringing Google's Gemini conversational AI assistant to all its cars, trucks, and SUVs starting in 2026. Tesla integrated xAI's Grok into its vehicles this summer, Mercedes rolled out ChatGPT integration, and Stellantis partnered with French AI firm Mistral for its own generative assistant. Now GM is playing catch-up with what could be its most significant tech partnership since adopting Android Automotive. The Gemini integration represents the next evolution of GM's existing "Google built-in" platform, which already powers infotainment systems across Buick, Chevrolet, Cadillac, and GMC vehicles with Google Assistant, Maps, and apps. According to GM executives at the event, the Gemini-powered assistant will handle far more sophisticated tasks than current voice commands. Drivers will be able to draft and send messages through natural conversation, plan complex routes with multiple stops including charging stations or coffee shops, and even prep for meetings while driving. The assistant promises deeper vehicle integration too. It'll access your car's data to provide maintenance alerts, explain features like one-pedal driving, and pre-condition your climate control before you get in. GM says users will control what information the AI can access, with the system learning from driving habits to offer personalized recommendations. The company was banned from the practice after public outcry, making data control promises crucial for consumer trust. Since 2023, the automaker has used Google Cloud's Dialogflow chatbot to handle non-emergency OnStar requests like routing and navigation help. The Gemini upgrade represents a massive leap in capabilities. Tesla's Grok integration gives drivers access to real-time information and conversational AI while driving. Mercedes' ChatGPT partnership, launched earlier this year, allows drivers to ask complex questions and get detailed responses through the MBUX infotainment system. Executives described the technology as "a mix of a health wearable and an AI pendant, but for your car" - suggesting the assistant will monitor vehicle health and driver patterns continuously rather than just responding to commands. The 2026 timeline puts GM slightly behind some competitors but ahead of others still developing AI strategies. More importantly, it aligns with GM's broader tech overhaul, which includes a complete electrical architecture redesign and automated driving features coming in 2028. For Google, this partnership extends Gemini's reach into the massive automotive market. With GM selling millions of vehicles annually across four major brands, the integration could put Gemini in front of more users than many smartphone apps. As cars become increasingly connected and autonomous, the quality of AI assistants could become as important as horsepower or fuel economy in consumer purchasing decisions. GM's bet on Gemini suggests the company believes conversational AI will be table stakes for automakers by the mid-2020s. GM's Gemini partnership signals the automotive industry's rapid shift toward AI-first vehicle experiences. While the 2026 launch puts GM slightly behind early movers like Tesla and Mercedes, the deep integration with existing Google services and OnStar infrastructure could give it a significant advantage. As conversational AI becomes standard in vehicles, GM's success will depend on execution - and whether drivers actually want their cars to be as chatty as their smartphones.

After letting users personalize the AI assistant's responses with data from Gmail, Search and YouTube, Google says it's bringing that same "Personal Intelligence" to Nano Banana 2 to make it easier for users to create personalized images with the AI model. The goal is to have the data affiliated with your Google account — your YouTube history, emails, Google Photos, etc. — provide context to Nano Banana 2 so you don't have to. Rather than prompting Gemini's image generation model with information about you or photos of your belongings, a direction to "create a picture of my desert island essentials" should produce an image that includes the things you care about without any extra context. Similarly, if you use labels in Google Photos to identify people or pets, you can tell Gemini to "create a hand-drawn illustration of mom," and it should be able to use Google Photo's labels to find the right reference photo and create an image of the right person. If Gemini creates images that don't look right, you can still send a follow-up prompt to refine the result, or select a new source image from Google Photos with the "+" button. Google says you can also click the "Sources" button to view what images the AI referenced in the first place, or ask it directly for the attribution and sources used for a specific image. Personalized user data is one of the unique advantages Google has over companies offering competing AI assistants, so expanding Personal Intelligence to an already popular feature like image generation is a natural way to build on that lead. For now, this more personalized version of Nano Banana 2 is available in the Gemini app for eligible AI Pro and AI Ultra subscribers. Google says the feature will come to Gemini in Chrome and other users "soon."
