In 2024, NPR reported on improperly redacted documents from another legal case that revealed that company employees sought to maximize teenagers' use of the app even while it publicly backed screentime limits for younger users. In one deposition , Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives. Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time. In an excerpt from a log of an internal chat Maher had with a colleague, which was read out in her testimony, she wrote: "I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn't think the harms are severe enough." Maher stated the company was aware of the sexual exploitation of minors on the platform before the Forbes article was published. An internal investigation found children between the ages of 13 and 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone, according to employees' testimony in the court filings. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption "Put simply, senior leaders know about this issue. There are some ongoing projects to fix parts of it, and frankly, I'm hoping [that] this article puts a fire behind other potential solutions," Maher wrote in an internal chat at the time a colleague. In 2021, TikTok introduced age-based account settings that restrict some features for 13 to 17-year-olds, including limits on sending and receiving direct messages and broadcasting in real time on TikTok Live. An internal investigation found children between the ages of 13 and 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone, according to employees' testimony in the March court filings. The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material. It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules. Federal law in the U.S. can impose criminal liability on a company for knowingly benefiting from participation in a child sex trafficking venture, said Silvija Krupena, director of the Financial Intelligence Unit at RedCompass Labs, a consultancy based in the U.K. "If an adult pays a child, through virtual gifts, for sexual acts on a livestream, that is payment for the sexual exploitation of a child. The gift is the payment," said Krupena. "Strip out the language of gifts, coins and diamonds, and the allegation is clear then. An adult paid. A child was exploited. The platform took a cut." Platforms must report apparent child sexual abuse material, child sex trafficking and online enticement to the nonprofit National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) when they obtain actual knowledge of facts indicating offenses covered by the reporting law. Money generated through child exploitation offences can be criminal proceeds. Knowingly processing those funds can amount to money laundering. If the gifting system qualifies as regulated money transmission, anti-money laundering obligations may follow. Knowledge matters a great deal, particularly when assessing potential criminal liability, which is why warnings to executives matter, said Krupena. In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions. TikTok said it has an anti-money laundering program in line with international standards and the industry's best practices. The company did not respond to requests for comment on whether it reported all of the TikTok Live videos containing child sexual abuse material to NCMEC, as required by federal law. The company also did not respond to questions about whether it had shut down the accounts it identified paying for child sexual abuse content. The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material. TikTok also did not answer questions about how it handled revenue it identified as coming from child sexual abuse material, including whether it forfeited those funds or retained them as profit. Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content. The app first became prominent in 2018, when ByteDance, TikTok's parent company, acquired Musical.ly, a platform for creating short music and lip-syncing videos that was popular with teen users in the U.S. Musical.ly was combined with TikTok, triggering rapid growth in the app's international user base. (As of January 22, 2026, TikTok's U.S. operations are majority-owned by American investors, following a deal that reduced ByteDance's control over the platform.) Soon after the 2018 merger with Musical.ly, the company was keen to determine the demographics of its user base in the U.S. But the court documents show that it held off on researching the question in an effort to avoid government scrutiny over having children under the age of 13 on the platform. In testimony concerning a 2018 discussion between Adam Wang, who was the Head of TikTok Live at the time, and Alex Zhu, co-founder of Musical.ly and then president of TikTok following the acquisition of Musical.ly, the two discussed a survey. They noted that "Having elementary school [as an answer in the survey] is definitely violating COPPA [the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act]," Wang confirmed in his testimony. Because of this, the survey avoided questions that could point to users' ages, such as what phase of schooling users were enrolled in. COPPA is a federal law that protects the online privacy and personal information of children under 13. It generally prohibits companies from collecting children's personal information without verifiable parental consent. TikTok said it notifies parents' accounts when a minor unlinks from family pairing. Among the most serious concerns raised in the testimony was TikTok's handling of content related to suicide and self-harm for young users. Testimony from Eric Han , who was TikTok's head of safety from April 2019 through June 2023, detailed internal chats he'd engaged in concerning "rabbit holes" — the company's term for when the algorithm gets stuck showing the user the same type of content over and over again. Han said he became aware of this problem in April 2020, and acknowledged that rabbit holes could be harmful, such as ones focusing on body image or suicide, and could violate TikTok's policies. An internal report authored and circulated by Han in 2020 and discussed in his testimony stated that there is a "Real contagion effect. Suicidal ideation and behavior, and the way that it is talked about on the platform." In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively." Despite this, Han said the platform did not warn parents of the potential dangers of TikTok.

They also flagged that users under 18 were using loopholes to bypass age-restricted content and to block parents and guardians from reviewing their activity on the app. TikTok also refrained from conducting surveys to assess the ages of its users because it was concerned that it would have to turn the results over to the Federal Trade Commission, the documents show.

NPR repeatedly sought comment from TikTok about the issues raised in the court documents. After extended communications, the company initially declined to provide a statement for this story. It did, however, direct NPR to various company policies that it had previously published on its website.

After publication, TikTok spokesperson Nathaniel Brown sent a statement saying the citations and claims in the story are "clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works."

Because the cases against TikTok have yet to be heard before a jury, the previously unreported employee depositions reviewed by NPR have not been submitted as evidence at trial. In 2024, NPR reported on improperly redacted documents from another legal case that revealed that company employees sought to maximize teenagers' use of the app even while it publicly backed screentime limits for younger users.

In one deposition , Reagen Maher, who held senior roles in safety and investigations at TikTok between 2021 and 2024, described going on a "crusade" for several months trying to elevate safety issues with some of TikTok's highest executives. Maher testified that her findings had been escalated to V Pappas, TikTok's chief operating officer at the time.

In an excerpt from a log of an internal chat Maher had with a colleague, which was read out in her testimony, she wrote: "I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn't think the harms are severe enough."
Maher stated the company was aware of the sexual exploitation of minors on the platform before the Forbes article was published.

An internal investigation found children between the ages of 13 and 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone, according to employees' testimony in the court filings. Mario Tama/Getty Images hide caption

"Put simply, senior leaders know about this issue. There are some ongoing projects to fix parts of it, and frankly, I'm hoping [that] this article puts a fire behind other potential solutions," Maher wrote in an internal chat at the time a colleague.

In 2021, TikTok introduced age-based account settings that restrict some features for 13 to 17-year-olds, including limits on sending and receiving direct messages and broadcasting in real time on TikTok Live.
An internal investigation found children between the ages of 13 and 15 appeared in 112,000 TikTok Live videos in January 2022 alone, according to employees' testimony in the March court filings.

The report identified risks including adult predators grooming children and the creation of child sexual abuse material. It also found that TikTok received "significant revenue" from gifts sent to livestreams that violated the platform's rules.

Federal law in the U.S. can impose criminal liability on a company for knowingly benefiting from participation in a child sex trafficking venture, said Silvija Krupena, director of the Financial Intelligence Unit at RedCompass Labs, a consultancy based in the U.K.

"If an adult pays a child, through virtual gifts, for sexual acts on a livestream, that is payment for the sexual exploitation of a child. The gift is the payment," said Krupena. "Strip out the language of gifts, coins and diamonds, and the allegation is clear then. An adult paid. A child was exploited. The platform took a cut."

Platforms must report apparent child sexual abuse material, child sex trafficking and online enticement to the nonprofit National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) when they obtain actual knowledge of facts indicating offenses covered by the reporting law.
Money generated through child exploitation offences can be criminal proceeds. Knowingly processing those funds can amount to money laundering.

If the gifting system qualifies as regulated money transmission, anti-money laundering obligations may follow. Knowledge matters a great deal, particularly when assessing potential criminal liability, which is why warnings to executives matter, said Krupena.
In an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024, Utah's attorney general alleged that TikTok's Live feature exposed minors to sexual exploitation by adults, while TikTok profited from the transactions.
TikTok said it has an anti-money laundering program in line with international standards and the industry's best practices.

The company did not respond to requests for comment on whether it reported all of the TikTok Live videos containing child sexual abuse material to NCMEC, as required by federal law. The company also did not respond to questions about whether it had shut down the accounts it identified paying for child sexual abuse content.

The company did not respond to NPR's questions about its anti-money laundering protocols, including whether it filed suspicious activity reports to the Treasury Department's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network related to the revenues it received from TikTok Live videos containing illegal material. TikTok also did not answer questions about how it handled revenue it identified as coming from child sexual abuse material, including whether it forfeited those funds or retained them as profit.
Other employee testimony highlighted TikTok's difficulties in preventing users under 18 from accessing adult-only features and harmful content.

The app first became prominent in 2018, when ByteDance, TikTok's parent company, acquired Musical.ly, a platform for creating short music and lip-syncing videos that was popular with teen users in the U.S. Musical.ly was combined with TikTok, triggering rapid growth in the app's international user base. (As of January 22, 2026, TikTok's U.S. operations are majority-owned by American investors, following a deal that reduced ByteDance's control over the platform.)

Soon after the 2018 merger with Musical.ly, the company was keen to determine the demographics of its user base in the U.S. But the court documents show that it held off on researching the question in an effort to avoid government scrutiny over having children under the age of 13 on the platform.

In testimony concerning a 2018 discussion between Adam Wang, who was the Head of TikTok Live at the time, and Alex Zhu, co-founder of Musical.ly and then president of TikTok following the acquisition of Musical.ly, the two discussed a survey. They noted that "Having elementary school [as an answer in the survey] is definitely violating COPPA [the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act]," Wang confirmed in his testimony. Because of this, the survey avoided questions that could point to users' ages, such as what phase of schooling users were enrolled in.

COPPA is a federal law that protects the online privacy and personal information of children under 13. It generally prohibits companies from collecting children's personal information without verifiable parental consent.
TikTok said it notifies parents' accounts when a minor unlinks from family pairing.
Among the most serious concerns raised in the testimony was TikTok's handling of content related to suicide and self-harm for young users.

Testimony from Eric Han , who was TikTok's head of safety from April 2019 through June 2023, detailed internal chats he'd engaged in concerning "rabbit holes" — the company's term for when the algorithm gets stuck showing the user the same type of content over and over again.
Han said he became aware of this problem in April 2020, and acknowledged that rabbit holes could be harmful, such as ones focusing on body image or suicide, and could violate TikTok's policies.

An internal report authored and circulated by Han in 2020 and discussed in his testimony stated that there is a "Real contagion effect. Suicidal ideation and behavior, and the way that it is talked about on the platform."

In a draft of TikTok's 2020 "Minor Safety Policy Annual Review", which was also quoted in Han's deposition, included bullet points stating: "Social media is inherently dangerous, and all minors are at risk when they engage on the platform" and "Minor Safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively."
Despite this, Han said the platform did not warn parents of the potential dangers of TikTok.

facts.text: Depositions of employees filed in March 2026 are shedding new light on TikTok's child safety practices.
TikTok was repeatedly warned by employees about the risks the social media platform posed to children, according to court records obtained by NPR .
The documents say employees were frustrated with how executives responded to their concerns about risks to children, including sexual exploitation and exposure to suicide-related content.

According to NPR, TikTok employees warned that minors were appearing in sexual content that was available for purchase on TikTok, raising concerns that the company could profit from potentially illegal activity.
TikTok, in addition to Meta, Google, and Snap, faces hundreds of lawsuits consolidated in federal court.
The lawsuits allege that these companies' platforms harm minors and that they failed to disclose known risks to young users.

"These citations and claims are clearly cherry-picked at the behest of trial lawyers and used to inaccurately rewrite our history and mislead the public about our commitment to youth safety and how our platform works," a TikTok spokesperson said in an emailed statement to TechCrunch.
"It's unfortunate that NPR has chosen to ignore the numerous documents and resources we have provided that demonstrate how these claims mischaracterize our record and platform features."
Additionally, the court documents show that TikTok didn't conduct surveys to determine the age of its users out of concern that it would have to share the results with the Federal Trade Commission.

It has not been an easy couple of weeks for the artificial intelligence giant Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), whose stock has fallen by over 9%. AI concerns have been front and center, as Anthropic appears to be dragging its feet on its suspected initial public offering, and as investors fret about some of the balance sheets of debt-laden neoclouds. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Nvidia is still having a solid year, but the company has posted incredibly strong results in its first two quarterly reports and arguably hasn't been rewarded as much as some investors would have expected. Earlier today, Reuters, citing anonymous sources, reported that Chinese companies, including ByteDance, Alibaba , and Tencent, have ordered more than 3 million Nvidia Blackwell chips, collectively worth $35 billion. Here's why that could be great news for the stock. After the Trump administration imposed new tariffs on China in 2025, it told Nvidia in April of that year that it would need to obtain an export license to continue selling data center chips to Chinese companies. This had also been an issue in former President Joe Biden's administration, with both administrations citing national security concerns. However, Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang, met with Trump on several occasions and also lobbied Washington regulators, eventually striking a deal in which Nvidia would cede 15% of its Chinese chip sales to the government. Most of those reports came last year, and there hasn't been much of an update since. Still, due to reservations from both U.S. and Chinese regulators, sales have hardly resumed. Nvidia's CFO Colette Kress said on the company's most recent earnings call at the end of August that less than 1% of Nvidia's data center revenue came from customers in China, and it was for Nvidia's older-generation Hopper 200 chips. extraction.body: ByteDance Ltd (字節跳動), Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (阿里巴巴) and Tencent Holdings Ltd (騰訊) have ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia Corp’s new RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards with a collective sticker price of over US$35 billion, two people familiar with the matter said, in a rush for a less powerful but export-compliant chip amid US restrictions on trade with China. US-based chipmaker Nvidia has told customers and partners it cannot guarantee that it can fill the orders because demand from Chinese technology companies far exceeds planned production, the two sources and a third person familiar with the matter said. They requested anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the media. The RTX PRO 5500 is a workstation chip, designed for powerful professional computers rather than the large data center clusters that use Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) processors. But it is among the most powerful Nvidia chips that are still available to Chinese buyers. Nvidia’s Blackwell-based B300 data center chip is not allowed to be sold to Chinese buyers under US export controls, while exports of its Hopper-based H200 are reviewed on a case-by-case basis and are subject to licensing conditions. One source said Nvidia told partners they might receive only 5 percent to 10 percent of the quantities requested. Another said the company had indicated it could produce no more than 3 million RTX PRO 5500 cards globally next year. Total orders from customers in China have exceeded 6 million, two of the sources said. The three Chinese tech giants’ orders are for cards priced at about US$11,400 each, two of the sources said, giving them a potential combined value of more than US$35 billion. The scale of the orders, which have not been previously reported, underscores the ongoing appetite among Chinese companies for Nvidia hardware despite the US curbs. Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) has said the restrictions reduced Nvidia’s share of China’s AI data center chip market from a near monopoly to effectively nothing. But demand for the RTX PRO 5500 suggests Nvidia retains a sizeable potential market in China through less powerful products that may still be available. The surge in demand also highlights how US restrictions have tightened computing power supplies in the world’s second-largest economy as Chinese companies race to develop cutting-edge AI models and propel Beijing’s effort to deploy the technology across its industries. Huawei, in particular, has gained market share, though Chinese chipmakers have generally struggled to match leading American products, partly because separate restrictions have limited access to the foreign equipment that is used to make the most advanced semiconductors. An Nvidia spokesperson said Chinese producers of workstation chips and cards have experienced "unprecedented growth since 2022," when the curbs were first imposed. "US firms continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated US export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly a half a decade ago, and China’s own limit on US imports," the spokesperson said. ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment. Starting next year, Nvidia is expected to devote much of its capacity at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) to Rubin, its next-generation platform for large-scale data centres, rather than products like the RTX PRO 5500, two of the sources said. TSMC declined to comment. Nvidia has told customers to expect early samples in December, with commercial deliveries beginning in the first quarter of next year, they added. extraction.body: Chinese technology giants including ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million Nvidia graphics cards, according to a report, a volume worth more than 47 trillion won. Reuters said the orders show undiminished Chinese demand for Nvidia hardware despite U.S. restrictions. Reuters reported on the 20th, citing two people familiar with the matter, that the three companies had ordered a combined total of more than 3 million units of Nvidia's RTX PRO 5500 graphics card. The product costs about $11,400 (about 15 million won) per unit, putting the total at more than $35 billion (about 47 trillion won), the people said. The RTX PRO 5500, a graphics card designed for personal computers, has specifications similar to the RTX 6000D, which Nvidia built with reduced performance in the middle of last year to comply with U.S. export controls. With Washington restricting exports of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, Chinese buyers have turned to lower-performance chips as a second-best option. The Blackwell-based B300 chip, used mainly in artificial intelligence data centers, is barred from sale in China, and the Hopper-based H200 requires approval for each export. Chinese companies are in fact acquiring the RTX PRO 5500 for AI inference rather than for use in personal computers, the people said. Inference requires less computing power than training a model on vast amounts of data, meaning it can be run without the most advanced chips. It was discontinued little more than a year after its release, but its price inside China has since more than doubled, according to the people. With no clear end in sight for U.S. export controls and a persistent shortage of AI computing power, the RTX PRO 5500 has emerged as an attractive substitute given its similarity to the RTX 6000D. Including the 3 million units confirmed in this case, orders placed by Chinese companies for the RTX PRO 5500 have surpassed 6 million units, the people said. Nvidia's RTX PRO 5500 output in 2027 will reach at most about 3 million units. The company has told customers that it can deliver only about 5% to 10% of their ordered volumes, according to the report. Part of the gap reflects the sharp jump in demand, but it also stems from shifting priorities on Nvidia's production lines. From 2027, Nvidia is expected to allocate a substantial portion of its production capacity at Taiwan's TSMC to Rubin, its next-generation advanced chip for large-scale data centers, rather than to products such as the RTX PRO 5500.

extraction.body: Chinese tech giants Alibaba (BABA), Tencent (TCEHY), ByteDance and other Chinese companies have reportedly ordered over $70 billion worth of Nvidia’s (NVDA) new RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards amid U.S. export curbs that keep them from purchasing the company’s more powerful chips. According to a Reuters report, the three companies have ordered more than 3 million of the workstation ships, which come with a collective sticker price of over $35 billion. Moreover, the overall number of orders from Chinese customers has exceeded 6 million. On the flip side, the report added that Nvidia has told its partners that it cannot guarantee that it will be able to fill the orders because the demand that’s come in from Chinese companies has exceeded the planned production they had in place. One source said Nvidia may be able to deliver only 5% to 10% of the total order amount. NVDA stock edged 0.18% lower in pre-market trade on Tuesday amid broader market weakness. On Stocktwits, retail sentiment around the Jensen Huang-led company trended in ‘neutral’ territory, accompanied by ‘normal’ levels of chatter. US Export Restrictions Drive Demand For Nvidia’s Alternative GPUs The rush of chip orders comes amid U.S. export controls that prohibit Nvidia from selling its Blackwell-based B300 data-center chip to Chinese buyers. The sale of its older Hopper-based H200 chips is only approved on a case-by-case basis. The RTX PRO 5500 is a workstation graphics card that is less powerful than the H200 and B300. Those data-center chips are designed to be linked in large numbers for demanding AI training and deployment workloads. Chinese Tech Firms Seek GPUs For AI Inference Chinese companies are reportedly seeking the RTX PRO 5500 cards primarily for AI inference, or running trained models to generate responses to user queries. Inference generally requires less computing power than training AI models on massive datasets, making less powerful chips potentially suitable for some workloads. The reported orders highlight the demand for Nvidia hardware in China despite restrictions on sales of its most powerful processors. But the gap between the number of orders and Nvidia’s planned production raises questions about how much of that demand the company can ultimately fulfill. It has not been an easy couple of weeks for the artificial intelligence giant Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), whose stock has fallen by over 9%. AI concerns have been front and center, as Anthropic appears to be dragging its feet on its suspected initial public offering, and as investors fret about some of the balance sheets of debt-laden neoclouds. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Nvidia is still having a solid year, but the company has posted incredibly strong results in its first two quarterly reports and arguably hasn't been rewarded as much as some investors would have expected. Earlier today, Reuters, citing anonymous sources, reported that Chinese companies, including ByteDance, Alibaba , and Tencent, have ordered more than 3 million Nvidia Blackwell chips, collectively worth $35 billion. Here's why that could be great news for the stock. After the Trump administration imposed new tariffs on China in 2025, it told Nvidia in April of that year that it would need to obtain an export license to continue selling data center chips to Chinese companies. This had also been an issue in former President Joe Biden's administration, with both administrations citing national security concerns. However, Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang, met with Trump on several occasions and also lobbied Washington regulators, eventually striking a deal in which Nvidia would cede 15% of its Chinese chip sales to the government. Most of those reports came last year, and there hasn't been much of an update since. Still, due to reservations from both U.S. and Chinese regulators, sales have hardly resumed. Nvidia's CFO Colette Kress said on the company's most recent earnings call at the end of August that less than 1% of Nvidia's data center revenue came from customers in China, and it was for Nvidia's older-generation Hopper 200 chips. Kress also said that Hopper sales are dilutive to gross margins, so it's positive that the company is able to sell Blackwell chips to Chinese customers. The even better news for investors is that Nvidia has been providing forward guidance without including potential sales to Chinese companies. On the last quarterly call, Kress said the company is projecting revenue for the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027 to come in around $108 billion, so $35 billion is not an insignificant number. However, Reuters also reported that Nvidia may not be able to fulfill all Chinese orders because it had not planned for such production levels. One source told Reuters that Nvidia may only be able to fill 5% to 10% of orders and has capacity to produce at most 3 million Blackwell chips globally in 2027. Despite the news, Nvidia's stock only traded marginally higher as of 2:04 p.m. ET today, and the market was broadly in the green. The stock has had some difficulty gaining traction, despite reporting blowout numbers and guidance each quarter so far this year. Part of it likely has to do with Nvidia's roughly $5.2 trillion market cap and the fact that it's already guiding for 70% revenue growth in its fiscal year 2028. Investors are also nervous about the AI trade and whether companies can keep buying chips at the same level they have been. Still, it's hard to view the demand in China as anything but broadly good news for Nvidia and the AI trade on the whole. It has not been an easy couple of weeks for the artificial intelligence giant Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), whose stock has fallen by over 9%.

AI concerns have been front and center, as Anthropic appears to be dragging its feet on its suspected initial public offering, and as investors fret about some of the balance sheets of debt-laden neoclouds.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Nvidia is still having a solid year, but the company has posted incredibly strong results in its first two quarterly reports and arguably hasn't been rewarded as much as some investors would have expected.

Earlier today, Reuters, citing anonymous sources, reported that Chinese companies, including ByteDance, Alibaba , and Tencent, have ordered more than 3 million Nvidia Blackwell chips, collectively worth $35 billion.
Here's why that could be great news for the stock.

After the Trump administration imposed new tariffs on China in 2025, it told Nvidia in April of that year that it would need to obtain an export license to continue selling data center chips to Chinese companies.
This had also been an issue in former President Joe Biden's administration, with both administrations citing national security concerns.

However, Nvidia's CEO, Jensen Huang, met with Trump on several occasions and also lobbied Washington regulators, eventually striking a deal in which Nvidia would cede 15% of its Chinese chip sales to the government.
Most of those reports came last year, and there hasn't been much of an update since. Still, due to reservations from both U.S. and Chinese regulators, sales have hardly resumed.

Nvidia's CFO Colette Kress said on the company's most recent earnings call at the end of August that less than 1% of Nvidia's data center revenue came from customers in China, and it was for Nvidia's older-generation Hopper 200 chips.
Kress also said that Hopper sales are dilutive to gross margins, so it's positive that the company is able to sell Blackwell chips to Chinese customers.

The even better news for investors is that Nvidia has been providing forward guidance without including potential sales to Chinese companies. On the last quarterly call, Kress said the company is projecting revenue for the third quarter of its fiscal year 2027 to come in around $108 billion, so $35 billion is not an insignificant number.

However, Reuters also reported that Nvidia may not be able to fulfill all Chinese orders because it had not planned for such production levels. One source told Reuters that Nvidia may only be able to fill 5% to 10% of orders and has capacity to produce at most 3 million Blackwell chips globally in 2027.

Despite the news, Nvidia's stock only traded marginally higher as of 2:04 p.m. ET today, and the market was broadly in the green. The stock has had some difficulty gaining traction, despite reporting blowout numbers and guidance each quarter so far this year.

Part of it likely has to do with Nvidia's roughly $5.2 trillion market cap and the fact that it's already guiding for 70% revenue growth in its fiscal year 2028. Investors are also nervous about the AI trade and whether companies can keep buying chips at the same level they have been.
Still, it's hard to view the demand in China as anything but broadly good news for Nvidia and the AI trade on the whole.

extraction.body: ByteDance Ltd (字節跳動), Alibaba Group Holding Ltd (阿里巴巴) and Tencent Holdings Ltd (騰訊) have ordered more than 3 million of Nvidia Corp’s new RTX PRO 5500 graphics cards with a collective sticker price of over US$35 billion, two people familiar with the matter said, in a rush for a less powerful but export-compliant chip amid US restrictions on trade with China. US-based chipmaker Nvidia has told customers and partners it cannot guarantee that it can fill the orders because demand from Chinese technology companies far exceeds planned production, the two sources and a third person familiar with the matter said. They requested anonymity because they are not authorized to speak to the media. The RTX PRO 5500 is a workstation chip, designed for powerful professional computers rather than the large data center clusters that use Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence (AI) processors. But it is among the most powerful Nvidia chips that are still available to Chinese buyers. Nvidia’s Blackwell-based B300 data center chip is not allowed to be sold to Chinese buyers under US export controls, while exports of its Hopper-based H200 are reviewed on a case-by-case basis and are subject to licensing conditions. One source said Nvidia told partners they might receive only 5 percent to 10 percent of the quantities requested. Another said the company had indicated it could produce no more than 3 million RTX PRO 5500 cards globally next year. Total orders from customers in China have exceeded 6 million, two of the sources said. The three Chinese tech giants’ orders are for cards priced at about US$11,400 each, two of the sources said, giving them a potential combined value of more than US$35 billion. The scale of the orders, which have not been previously reported, underscores the ongoing appetite among Chinese companies for Nvidia hardware despite the US curbs. Nvidia chief executive officer Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) has said the restrictions reduced Nvidia’s share of China’s AI data center chip market from a near monopoly to effectively nothing. But demand for the RTX PRO 5500 suggests Nvidia retains a sizeable potential market in China through less powerful products that may still be available. The surge in demand also highlights how US restrictions have tightened computing power supplies in the world’s second-largest economy as Chinese companies race to develop cutting-edge AI models and propel Beijing’s effort to deploy the technology across its industries. Huawei, in particular, has gained market share, though Chinese chipmakers have generally struggled to match leading American products, partly because separate restrictions have limited access to the foreign equipment that is used to make the most advanced semiconductors. An Nvidia spokesperson said Chinese producers of workstation chips and cards have experienced "unprecedented growth since 2022," when the curbs were first imposed. "US firms continue to be restricted by a combination of outdated US export controls, which cover gaming products released nearly a half a decade ago, and China’s own limit on US imports," the spokesperson said. ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent did not respond to requests for comment. Starting next year, Nvidia is expected to devote much of its capacity at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電) to Rubin, its next-generation platform for large-scale data centres, rather than products like the RTX PRO 5500, two of the sources said. TSMC declined to comment. Nvidia has told customers to expect early samples in December, with commercial deliveries beginning in the first quarter of next year, they added. passages: Chinese technology giants including ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million Nvidia graphics cards, according to a report, a volume worth more than 47 trillion won.
Reuters said the orders show undiminished Chinese demand for Nvidia hardware despite U.S. restrictions.
With Washington restricting exports of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, Chinese buyers have turned to lower-performance chips as a second-best option.

extraction.body: Chinese technology giants including ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million Nvidia graphics cards, according to a report, a volume worth more than 47 trillion won. Reuters said the orders show undiminished Chinese demand for Nvidia hardware despite U.S. restrictions. Reuters reported on the 20th, citing two people familiar with the matter, that the three companies had ordered a combined total of more than 3 million units of Nvidia's RTX PRO 5500 graphics card. The product costs about $11,400 (about 15 million won) per unit, putting the total at more than $35 billion (about 47 trillion won), the people said. The RTX PRO 5500, a graphics card designed for personal computers, has specifications similar to the RTX 6000D, which Nvidia built with reduced performance in the middle of last year to comply with U.S. export controls. With Washington restricting exports of Nvidia's most advanced chips to China, Chinese buyers have turned to lower-performance chips as a second-best option. The Blackwell-based B300 chip, used mainly in artificial intelligence data centers, is barred from sale in China, and the Hopper-based H200 requires approval for each export. Chinese companies are in fact acquiring the RTX PRO 5500 for AI inference rather than for use in personal computers, the people said. Inference requires less computing power than training a model on vast amounts of data, meaning it can be run without the most advanced chips. It was discontinued little more than a year after its release, but its price inside China has since more than doubled, according to the people. With no clear end in sight for U.S. export controls and a persistent shortage of AI computing power, the RTX PRO 5500 has emerged as an attractive substitute given its similarity to the RTX 6000D. Including the 3 million units confirmed in this case, orders placed by Chinese companies for the RTX PRO 5500 have surpassed 6 million units, the people said. Nvidia's RTX PRO 5500 output in 2027 will reach at most about 3 million units. The company has told customers that it can deliver only about 5% to 10% of their ordered volumes, according to the report. Part of the gap reflects the sharp jump in demand, but it also stems from shifting priorities on Nvidia's production lines. From 2027, Nvidia is expected to allocate a substantial portion of its production capacity at Taiwan's TSMC to Rubin, its next-generation advanced chip for large-scale data centers, rather than to products such as the RTX PRO 5500.

sources.title: OpenAI acquires startup Orchestra Bio⁠ to beef up its biotech business
passages: OpenAI on Tuesday acquired a four-year-old AI biotech software startup called Orchestra Bio, the company announced via its website.
Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the startup had reportedly raised around $20 million as of 2025 from backers like Andreessen Horowitz, Atria, and 8VC.
The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma.
In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors.
In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind , its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results.
OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.
Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

passages: OpenAI is buying its way into one of the slowest industries on Earth.

On October 20, 2026, the company announced it has acquired Orchestra Bio, a startup that uses AI to streamline how biopharma teams develop drugs. 
 Moving a drug from discovery to market in the US can take anywhere from 10 to 15 years. 
 

 What OpenAI is actually buying 
 Orchestra Bio built a platform that lets humans and AI agents jointly manage drug programs. 
 The company describes its product as an “agentic operating layer” that spans multiple stages of drug development.
Orchestra Bio was founded around October 2022 by Ashoka Rajendra.
The company received seed financing in late 2022, with a round led by investors including Jay Rughani.
That puts the startup’s journey from seed round to acquisition at roughly four years.
OpenAI plans to combine Orchestra’s platform with its existing Rosalind suite.
Rosalind includes models built for biological and chemical reasoning, along with data analysis tools.
Acquiring Orchestra pushes OpenAI’s strategy further.
Instead of selling models to biopharma teams and hoping they wire them into their workflows, OpenAI can now offer the workflow itself.
The key things to watch are how quickly OpenAI integrates Orchestra into Rosalind and whether the promised specialized agents materialize as products biopharma teams actually adopt.

Moving a drug from discovery to market in the US can take anywhere from 10 to 15 years.
Orchestra Bio built a platform that lets humans and AI agents jointly manage drug programs.

The company describes its product as an “agentic operating layer” that spans multiple stages of drug development. It is software that sits on top of a drug program and coordinates work across phases, with AI agents handling tasks alongside human scientists.
OpenAI plans to combine Orchestra’s platform with its existing Rosalind suite. Rosalind includes models built for biological and chemical reasoning, along with data analysis tools.

The acquisition is a classic example of how the biggest AI labs (namely OpenAI and Anthropic) are building ever more software for the biggest industries, like pharma.
In the startup world, there is an ongoing fear that at any moment, the labs will launch new features and become competitors.
In this case, Orchestra is getting absorbed, rather than stomped out.

OpenAI says it’s adding Orchestra’s team and technology to work on Rosalind , its AI model for life sciences research, and to its related Rosalind Workbench tool, a harness that aims to help researchers plan experiments and analyze results.
OpenAI has already won some big names as customers for Rosalind, including, it says, Moderna⁠ and Novo Nordisk⁠.
Orchestra creates AI agents that help biotech companies manage the minutiae of drug discovery operations, from tracking finances to resolving scheduling issues with clinical trials.

sources.title: OpenAI acquires biotech startup Orchestra Bio to push into drug development - Crypto Briefing
passages: OpenAI is buying its way into one of the slowest industries on Earth.

On October 20, 2026, the company announced it has acquired Orchestra Bio, a startup that uses AI to streamline how biopharma teams develop drugs. 
 Moving a drug from discovery to market in the US can take anywhere from 10 to 15 years. 
 

 What OpenAI is actually buying 
 Orchestra Bio built a platform that lets humans and AI agents jointly manage drug programs. 
 The company describes its product as an “agentic operating layer” that spans multiple stages of drug development.
Orchestra Bio was founded around October 2022 by Ashoka Rajendra.
The company received seed financing in late 2022, with a round led by investors including Jay Rughani.
That puts the startup’s journey from seed round to acquisition at roughly four years.
OpenAI plans to combine Orchestra’s platform with its existing Rosalind suite.
Rosalind includes models built for biological and chemical reasoning, along with data analysis tools.
Acquiring Orchestra pushes OpenAI’s strategy further.
Instead of selling models to biopharma teams and hoping they wire them into their workflows, OpenAI can now offer the workflow itself.
The key things to watch are how quickly OpenAI integrates Orchestra into Rosalind and whether the promised specialized agents materialize as products biopharma teams actually adopt.

sources.title: ChatGPT now lets you lock your chats
passages: OpenAI announced on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device.
Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices.
The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for personal conversations .
Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled.
Locked Chats will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans.
The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare.
Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results.
With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section.
That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats.
OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN.

sources.title: You Can Now Lock Your Private ChatGPT Conversations With a PIN
passages: If you have personal conversations with ChatGPT that you don't want others to see, you can now add an extra layer of security for those specific chats.

You can repeat this with any existing conversation or start a locked chat from scratch under Projects > Locked Chats by entering your PIN or authentication method and typing a message to launch the chat.
Select Lock chat > Lock chat and create or enter your account PIN.
Select Create a PIN, enter your four-digit code, and enter it again to confirm.

As the support page notes, locked chats are not encrypted end to end or placed in a separate encrypted vault, and locking a chat does not affect other privacy settings, such as Improve the model for everyone (which can be turned off in Settings > Data controls) or remove information ChatGPT already knows about you.
However, once locked, they are hidden from your regular chat history, pinned chats, and regular conversation search.
This moves the conversation to your locked chats project.
There are other limitations, too: For example, temporary, archived, and group chats can't be locked, nor can those with shared links, scheduled and background tasks, or meeting recordings.

extraction.body: If you have personal conversations with ChatGPT that you don't want others to see, you can now add an extra layer of security for those specific chats. The new Locked Chats feature allows you to hide sensitive conversations behind a four-digit account PIN (or biometric authentication on mobile), meaning others with access to your device or screen can't read them. Locked chats are retained in your chat history—unlike temporary chats, which are private conversations that aren't saved by default—so you can return to or continue them at any point. However, once locked, they are hidden from your regular chat history, pinned chats, and regular conversation search. To access them, you have to go to Projects > Locked chats and enter your PIN or device unlock method (such as Face ID or Touch ID). How to set up Locked Chats on ChatGPTTo start a locked chat for the first time, open an existing conversation that you want to keep private and open the options menu. Select Lock chat > Lock chat and create or enter your account PIN. This moves the conversation to your locked chats project. You can repeat this with any existing conversation or start a locked chat from scratch under Projects > Locked Chats by entering your PIN or authentication method and typing a message to launch the chat. When you're done, select Lock now to end access to locked chats and hide them from the sidebar. Note that if you don't already have an account PIN set up, you should be prompted to do so the first time you attempt to lock a chat. Select Create a PIN, enter your four-digit code, and enter it again to confirm. If you reset your account PIN at any point, all locked chats are permanently deleted and cannot be recovered. Locked chats are available on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans on both mobile and desktop apps. The feature is not available for ChatGPT for Healthcare. There are other limitations, too: For example, temporary, archived, and group chats can't be locked, nor can those with shared links, scheduled and background tasks, or meeting recordings. OpenAI says locked chats are rolling out gradually, so they may not be available to all users yet. Locked chats are not encryptedWhile locked chats do add a layer of privacy in terms of how conversations appear on your device, they are not suddenly encrypted or otherwise protected from being retained or used by OpenAI. As the support page notes, locked chats are not encrypted end to end or placed in a separate encrypted vault, and locking a chat does not affect other privacy settings, such as Improve the model for everyone (which can be turned off in Settings > Data controls) or remove information ChatGPT already knows about you.

extraction.body: In an era that is driven by artificial intelligence, chatbots are no longer just tools to generate images for you. They have become therapists, diaries, and your assistant that collect your data silently. From Google Gemini to ChatGPT, these platforms store your preferences, prompts, and even note behavioural patterns to improve the customised results they offer you. You might be offering your data to train the AI tools. In this article, we explore how you can take back control and disable settings that may store your data by AI chatbots. How To Lock Down Data On ChatGPT Turn off model training: Go to Settings > Switch off ‘Improve the model for everyone’. Use Temporary Chats: Start a temporary chat session. Delete your chat history manually, or clear the entire history regularly on a monthly basis. How To Lock Down Data On Google Gemini Google Gemini can take your emails and documents alongside other media, since it is mostly connected to Drive, Gmail, and other Google services. Disable the Gemini Apps Activity Visit the Gemini Apps Activity settings > Toggle off data collection. Set Auto-delete for data Choose auto-delete (every three months is recommended). How To Lock Down Data On Microsoft Copilot The Microsoft Copilot depends on whether you are using the services for personal use or work account: Disable The Model Training Go to Profile > Visit Settings > Click on Privacy. Disable Personalisation Prevent Copilot from remembering your data by disabling the memory features.

extraction.body: OpenAI announced on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device. Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices. Unlike the app’s Temporary Chats, which provide a separate session that doesn’t appear in chat history, users can return to Locked Chats at any time. The company says the feature is designed for situations where users might be discussing something personal or planning a surprise and want to keep those conversations private when handing their device to friends or family to show them something in another chat. The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for personal conversations . Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled. OpenAI notes that locking a chat doesn’t create end-to-end encryption or a separate encrypted vault, change how long it retains the chat, remove information that ChatGPT remembered before a chat was locked, or change the “Improve the model for everyone” setting. Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results. With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section. New messages sent after locking a chat can update that memory, but don’t update regular Memory. That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats. OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN. Additionally, the Locked Chats option isn’t available for temporary chats, archived chats, group chats, chats created from a shared link, chats with scheduled tasks, and chats with meeting recordings. Locked Chats will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans. The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare. The feature is starting to roll out on Tuesday, so it may not be live yet for all users. story.title: ChatGPT now lets you lock your chats

facts.text: OpenAI announced on Tuesday that users can now lock ChatGPT conversations to keep sensitive chats private when others may have access to their screen or device.
Users can secure their locked chats with a four-digit PIN, or use Face ID or Touch ID on supported devices.
The addition of locked chats adds a new layer of privacy to ChatGPT, as the app is increasingly used for personal conversations .
Of course, while locking a chat can limit access, it doesn’t address concerns about how sensitive information is stored or handled.
Locked Chats will be available to users on ChatGPT Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise, and Edu plans.
The company notes that the feature is not available on ChatGPT for Healthcare.
Once users lock a chat, it moves to a dedicated “Locked Chats” section, where it’s kept separate from regular chat history, pinned conversations, and chat search results.
With Memory enabled, Locked Chats has its own separate memory shared across conversations within the section.
That means new information from locked chats won’t leak into regular chats.
OpenAI says resetting a PIN permanently deletes all locked chats, files, and other content protected by the previous PIN.
There are some questions about how locked chats might interact with ChatGPT’s memory and recall features.
ChatGPT already offers temporary chats for conversations that are more personal or sensitive.

As OpenAI and ChatGPT continue to evolve and improve, a latest upgrade could allow the app to lock your most sensitive chats behind a PIN code or fingerprint scan, preventing anyone from catching a glimpse of them.
References to the upcoming feature include “locked chats” and “Protect chats” in the code.
Information about the potential feature is based on inactive code found in the latest version of ChatGPT for Android, as spotted by Android Authority.
These chats are instantly forgotten once you close them, disappearing from your ChatGPT account.

From private queries and medical questions to job applications, the new feature could keep sensitive conversations better protected.
This is where a dedicated lock for individual conversations could prove useful.

The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution has produced two of the fastest-growing start-ups in history. OpenAI burst onto the scene in late 2022 when it launched ChatGPT, introducing consumers around the world to generative AI. Meanwhile, Anthropic has emerged as a formidable competitor with its Claude models. Both companies' growth has been extraordinary. Following a $122 billion funding round in March, OpenAI reached a valuation of $852 billion, while Anthropic was valued at $965 billion after its Series H round in May. Naturally, AI investors are eager to know when they can buy shares. Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Anthropic confidentially filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in June and could make its public debut as soon as next month. OpenAI has also explored going public, although its timing remains uncertain. Here's an interesting alternative: Rather than waiting for either company to go public at a valuation approaching the trillion-dollar milestone, investors can buy Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) instead. Alphabet stands to benefit regardless of which AI developer ultimately wins. Read on to learn why. One of Alphabet's quiet advantages is that it doesn't need its Gemini AI models to beat ChatGPT or Claude. That reason is Google Cloud provides compute infrastructure to its competitors. In May 2025, OpenAI agreed to use Google Cloud's capacity to train and deploy its AI models. This relationship is particularly interesting because up to that point, OpenAI was primarily tied to Microsoft Azure. Adding Google provided OpenAI with an alternative source of AI compute while giving Alphabet a hyperscaler customer whose infrastructure requirements are enormous. Anthropic's relationship with Google runs even deeper. In October 2025, Anthropic announced its use of Google's custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). In April, this relationship was expanded to include multiple gigawatts of TPU capacity expected to come online in 2027. These arrangements create an attractive business model for Alphabet because the company can develop AI products for consumers while simultaneously supplying infrastructure that competing enterprises need. The strategy is already producing impressive results. During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. While not all of that growth came from OpenAI and Anthropic, their expanding infrastructure commitments underscore why Google Cloud should remain a major beneficiary of the AI boom. Alphabet isn't just an infrastructure partner to Anthropic. It's also one of the company's largest investors. Google initially invested in Anthropic in 2023. But by early 2026, Alphabet had invested roughly $3 billion in Anthropic and owned an estimated 14% equity stake. In April, Google announced plans to invest up to another $40 billion. The deal was structured to include an initial $10 billion commitment, with an additional $30 billion contingent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. Why is Google investing so heavily in a company whose generative models compete directly with Gemini? The answer is simple: Alphabet is positioned to benefit from Anthropic's success in multiple ways. First, its equity investment will appreciate as Anthropic's valuation increases. Additionally, Anthropic is a major customer for Google's cloud infrastructure and custom AI chips. Third, Google's tie-up with Anthropic gives it exposure to an alternative AI ecosystem, reducing its dependence on Gemini emerging as the industry's go-to model. This is an unusually versatile position to be in. If Anthropic goes public at its reported $2 trillion valuation, a hypothetical 14% stake would be worth $280 billion. This shows how Alphabet can participate in one of the largest IPOs in history without investors needing to lift a finger and buy Anthropic stock directly. OpenAI's valuation of $852 billion represents approximately 17 times its reported $50 billion annualized revenue run rate. Meanwhile, Anthropic's $965 billion valuation represents 14 times its Q3 annualized revenue run rate of $67.2 billion. At a $2 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would trade at nearly 30 times its current revenue run rate. These are enormous premiums, especially considering the capital expenditures required to develop advanced AI. Moreover, OpenAI remains unprofitable while Anthropic recently reported a small profit on an adjusted operating basis. Alphabet offers a much different financial profile. During Q2, the company generated $120 billion in revenue and roughly $40.8 billion in operating income. Alphabet stock trades around a 23 times forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio -- a relatively reasonable valuation considering its established and highly profitable advertising and cloud businesses. While OpenAI and Anthropic could become respected public companies, their anticipated valuations already reflect high expectations. Alphabet offers investors exposure to both AI developers through Google Cloud, an existing equity stake in Anthropic, and its own growing AI ecosystem. Combined with its AI-driven revenue and robust profitability, I see Alphabet as the more compelling AI stock to buy and hold ahead of these anticipated mega-IPOs. extraction.body: The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution has produced two of the fastest-growing start-ups in history. OpenAI burst onto the scene in late 2022 when it launched ChatGPT, introducing consumers around the world to generative AI. Meanwhile, Anthropic has emerged as a formidable competitor with its Claude models. Both companies' growth has been extraordinary. Following a $122 billion funding round in March, OpenAI reached a valuation of $852 billion, while Anthropic was valued at $965 billion after its Series H round in May. Naturally, AI investors are eager to know when they can buy shares. Anthropic confidentially filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in June and could make its public debut as soon as next month. OpenAI has also explored going public, although its timing remains uncertain. Here's an interesting alternative: Rather than waiting for either company to go public at a valuation approaching the trillion-dollar milestone, investors can buy Alphabet ( GOOGL -1.14% ) ( GOOG -1.10% ) instead. Alphabet stands to benefit regardless of which AI developer ultimately wins. Read on to learn why. One of Alphabet's quiet advantages is that it doesn't need its Gemini AI models to beat ChatGPT or Claude. That reason is Google Cloud provides compute infrastructure to its competitors. In May 2025, OpenAI agreed to use Google Cloud's capacity to train and deploy its AI models. This relationship is particularly interesting because up to that point, OpenAI was primarily tied to Microsoft Azure. Adding Google provided OpenAI with an alternative source of AI compute while giving Alphabet a hyperscaler customer whose infrastructure requirements are enormous. Anthropic's relationship with Google runs even deeper. In October 2025, Anthropic announced its use of Google's custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). In April, this relationship was expanded to include multiple gigawatts of TPU capacity expected to come online in 2027. These arrangements create an attractive business model for Alphabet because the company can develop AI products for consumers while simultaneously supplying infrastructure that competing enterprises need. The strategy is already producing impressive results. During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. While not all of that growth came from OpenAI and Anthropic, their expanding infrastructure commitments underscore why Google Cloud should remain a major beneficiary of the AI boom. Alphabet isn't just an infrastructure partner to Anthropic. It's also one of the company's largest investors. Google initially invested in Anthropic in 2023. But by early 2026, Alphabet had invested roughly $3 billion in Anthropic and owned an estimated 14% equity stake. In April, Google announced plans to invest up to another $40 billion. The deal was structured to include an initial $10 billion commitment, with an additional $30 billion contingent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. Why is Google investing so heavily in a company whose generative models compete directly with Gemini? The answer is simple: Alphabet is positioned to benefit from Anthropic's success in multiple ways. First, its equity investment will appreciate as Anthropic's valuation increases. Additionally, Anthropic is a major customer for Google's cloud infrastructure and custom AI chips. Third, Google's tie-up with Anthropic gives it exposure to an alternative AI ecosystem, reducing its dependence on Gemini emerging as the industry's go-to model. This is an unusually versatile position to be in. If Anthropic goes public at its reported $2 trillion valuation, a hypothetical 14% stake would be worth $280 billion. This shows how Alphabet can participate in one of the largest IPOs in history without investors needing to lift a finger and buy Anthropic stock directly. OpenAI's valuation of $852 billion represents approximately 17 times its reported $50 billion annualized revenue run rate . Meanwhile, Anthropic's $965 billion valuation represents 14 times its Q3 annualized revenue run rate of $67.2 billion . At a $2 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would trade at nearly 30 times its current revenue run rate. These are enormous premiums, especially considering the capital expenditures required to develop advanced AI. Moreover, OpenAI remains unprofitable while Anthropic recently reported a small profit on an adjusted operating basis . Alphabet offers a much different financial profile. During Q2, the company generated $120 billion in revenue and roughly $40.8 billion in operating income. Alphabet stock trades around a 23 times forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio -- a relatively reasonable valuation considering its established and highly profitable advertising and cloud businesses. While OpenAI and Anthropic could become respected public companies, their anticipated valuations already reflect high expectations. Alphabet offers investors exposure to both AI developers through Google Cloud, an existing equity stake in Anthropic, and its own growing AI ecosystem. Combined with its AI-driven revenue and robust profitability, I see Alphabet as the more compelling AI stock to buy and hold ahead of these anticipated mega-IPOs. Why is Google investing so heavily in a company whose generative models compete directly with Gemini?

The answer is simple: Alphabet is positioned to benefit from Anthropic's success in multiple ways. First, its equity investment will appreciate as Anthropic's valuation increases. Additionally, Anthropic is a major customer for Google's cloud infrastructure and custom AI chips. Third, Google's tie-up with Anthropic gives it exposure to an alternative AI ecosystem, reducing its dependence on Gemini emerging as the industry's go-to model.

This is an unusually versatile position to be in. If Anthropic goes public at its reported $2 trillion valuation, a hypothetical 14% stake would be worth $280 billion. This shows how Alphabet can participate in one of the largest IPOs in history without investors needing to lift a finger and buy Anthropic stock directly.

OpenAI's valuation of $852 billion represents approximately 17 times its reported $50 billion annualized revenue run rate . Meanwhile, Anthropic's $965 billion valuation represents 14 times its Q3 annualized revenue run rate of $67.2 billion . At a $2 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would trade at nearly 30 times its current revenue run rate.

These are enormous premiums, especially considering the capital expenditures required to develop advanced AI. Moreover, OpenAI remains unprofitable while Anthropic recently reported a small profit on an adjusted operating basis .

Alphabet offers a much different financial profile. During Q2, the company generated $120 billion in revenue and roughly $40.8 billion in operating income. Alphabet stock trades around a 23 times forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio -- a relatively reasonable valuation considering its established and highly profitable advertising and cloud businesses.

While OpenAI and Anthropic could become respected public companies, their anticipated valuations already reflect high expectations. Alphabet offers investors exposure to both AI developers through Google Cloud, an existing equity stake in Anthropic, and its own growing AI ecosystem. Combined with its AI-driven revenue and robust profitability, I see Alphabet as the more compelling AI stock to buy and hold ahead of these anticipated mega-IPOs.

Anthropic confidentially filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in June and could make its public debut as soon as next month. OpenAI has also explored going public, although its timing remains uncertain.

Here's an interesting alternative: Rather than waiting for either company to go public at a valuation approaching the trillion-dollar milestone, investors can buy Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOGL) (NASDAQ: GOOG) instead. Alphabet stands to benefit regardless of which AI developer ultimately wins. Read on to learn why.

One of Alphabet's quiet advantages is that it doesn't need its Gemini AI models to beat ChatGPT or Claude. That reason is Google Cloud provides compute infrastructure to its competitors. In May 2025, OpenAI agreed to use Google Cloud's capacity to train and deploy its AI models.

This relationship is particularly interesting because up to that point, OpenAI was primarily tied to Microsoft Azure. Adding Google provided OpenAI with an alternative source of AI compute while giving Alphabet a hyperscaler customer whose infrastructure requirements are enormous.

Anthropic's relationship with Google runs even deeper. In October 2025, Anthropic announced its use of Google's custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). In April, this relationship was expanded to include multiple gigawatts of TPU capacity expected to come online in 2027.

These arrangements create an attractive business model for Alphabet because the company can develop AI products for consumers while simultaneously supplying infrastructure that competing enterprises need.

The strategy is already producing impressive results. During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. While not all of that growth came from OpenAI and Anthropic, their expanding infrastructure commitments underscore why Google Cloud should remain a major beneficiary of the AI boom.

Alphabet isn't just an infrastructure partner to Anthropic. It's also one of the company's largest investors. Google initially invested in Anthropic in 2023. But by early 2026, Alphabet had invested roughly $3 billion in Anthropic and owned an estimated 14% equity stake. In April, Google announced plans to invest up to another $40 billion. The deal was structured to include an initial $10 billion commitment, with an additional $30 billion contingent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones.
Why is Google investing so heavily in a company whose generative models compete directly with Gemini?

The answer is simple: Alphabet is positioned to benefit from Anthropic's success in multiple ways. First, its equity investment will appreciate as Anthropic's valuation increases. Additionally, Anthropic is a major customer for Google's cloud infrastructure and custom AI chips. Third, Google's tie-up with Anthropic gives it exposure to an alternative AI ecosystem, reducing its dependence on Gemini emerging as the industry's go-to model.

This is an unusually versatile position to be in. If Anthropic goes public at its reported $2 trillion valuation, a hypothetical 14% stake would be worth $280 billion. This shows how Alphabet can participate in one of the largest IPOs in history without investors needing to lift a finger and buy Anthropic stock directly.

OpenAI's valuation of $852 billion represents approximately 17 times its reported $50 billion annualized revenue run rate. Meanwhile, Anthropic's $965 billion valuation represents 14 times its Q3 annualized revenue run rate of $67.2 billion. At a $2 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would trade at nearly 30 times its current revenue run rate.

These are enormous premiums, especially considering the capital expenditures required to develop advanced AI. Moreover, OpenAI remains unprofitable while Anthropic recently reported a small profit on an adjusted operating basis.

Alphabet offers a much different financial profile. During Q2, the company generated $120 billion in revenue and roughly $40.8 billion in operating income. Alphabet stock trades around a 23 times forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio -- a relatively reasonable valuation considering its established and highly profitable advertising and cloud businesses.

While OpenAI and Anthropic could become respected public companies, their anticipated valuations already reflect high expectations. Alphabet offers investors exposure to both AI developers through Google Cloud, an existing equity stake in Anthropic, and its own growing AI ecosystem. Combined with its AI-driven revenue and robust profitability, I see Alphabet as the more compelling AI stock to buy and hold ahead of these anticipated mega-IPOs.
