extraction.body: The artificial intelligence (AI) revolution has produced two of the fastest-growing start-ups in history. OpenAI burst onto the scene in late 2022 when it launched ChatGPT, introducing consumers around the world to generative AI. Meanwhile, Anthropic has emerged as a formidable competitor with its Claude models. Both companies' growth has been extraordinary. Following a $122 billion funding round in March, OpenAI reached a valuation of $852 billion, while Anthropic was valued at $965 billion after its Series H round in May. Naturally, AI investors are eager to know when they can buy shares. Anthropic confidentially filed for an initial public offering (IPO) in June and could make its public debut as soon as next month. OpenAI has also explored going public, although its timing remains uncertain. Here's an interesting alternative: Rather than waiting for either company to go public at a valuation approaching the trillion-dollar milestone, investors can buy Alphabet ( GOOGL -1.14% ) ( GOOG -1.10% ) instead. Alphabet stands to benefit regardless of which AI developer ultimately wins. Read on to learn why. One of Alphabet's quiet advantages is that it doesn't need its Gemini AI models to beat ChatGPT or Claude. That reason is Google Cloud provides compute infrastructure to its competitors. In May 2025, OpenAI agreed to use Google Cloud's capacity to train and deploy its AI models. This relationship is particularly interesting because up to that point, OpenAI was primarily tied to Microsoft Azure. Adding Google provided OpenAI with an alternative source of AI compute while giving Alphabet a hyperscaler customer whose infrastructure requirements are enormous. Anthropic's relationship with Google runs even deeper. In October 2025, Anthropic announced its use of Google's custom silicon, called Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). In April, this relationship was expanded to include multiple gigawatts of TPU capacity expected to come online in 2027. These arrangements create an attractive business model for Alphabet because the company can develop AI products for consumers while simultaneously supplying infrastructure that competing enterprises need. The strategy is already producing impressive results. During the second quarter, Google Cloud revenue surged 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. While not all of that growth came from OpenAI and Anthropic, their expanding infrastructure commitments underscore why Google Cloud should remain a major beneficiary of the AI boom. Alphabet isn't just an infrastructure partner to Anthropic. It's also one of the company's largest investors. Google initially invested in Anthropic in 2023. But by early 2026, Alphabet had invested roughly $3 billion in Anthropic and owned an estimated 14% equity stake. In April, Google announced plans to invest up to another $40 billion. The deal was structured to include an initial $10 billion commitment, with an additional $30 billion contingent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. Why is Google investing so heavily in a company whose generative models compete directly with Gemini? The answer is simple: Alphabet is positioned to benefit from Anthropic's success in multiple ways. First, its equity investment will appreciate as Anthropic's valuation increases. Additionally, Anthropic is a major customer for Google's cloud infrastructure and custom AI chips. Third, Google's tie-up with Anthropic gives it exposure to an alternative AI ecosystem, reducing its dependence on Gemini emerging as the industry's go-to model. This is an unusually versatile position to be in. If Anthropic goes public at its reported $2 trillion valuation, a hypothetical 14% stake would be worth $280 billion. This shows how Alphabet can participate in one of the largest IPOs in history without investors needing to lift a finger and buy Anthropic stock directly. OpenAI's valuation of $852 billion represents approximately 17 times its reported $50 billion annualized revenue run rate . Meanwhile, Anthropic's $965 billion valuation represents 14 times its Q3 annualized revenue run rate of $67.2 billion . At a $2 trillion IPO valuation, Anthropic would trade at nearly 30 times its current revenue run rate. These are enormous premiums, especially considering the capital expenditures required to develop advanced AI. Moreover, OpenAI remains unprofitable while Anthropic recently reported a small profit on an adjusted operating basis . Alphabet offers a much different financial profile. During Q2, the company generated $120 billion in revenue and roughly $40.8 billion in operating income. Alphabet stock trades around a 23 times forward price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio -- a relatively reasonable valuation considering its established and highly profitable advertising and cloud businesses. While OpenAI and Anthropic could become respected public companies, their anticipated valuations already reflect high expectations. Alphabet offers investors exposure to both AI developers through Google Cloud, an existing equity stake in Anthropic, and its own growing AI ecosystem. Combined with its AI-driven revenue and robust profitability, I see Alphabet as the more compelling AI stock to buy and hold ahead of these anticipated mega-IPOs. Your guide to Netflix, Disney Plus, Hulu and more When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works . What is JustWatch? If you’ve ever scoured the internet to find which TV streaming service has a specific film or series available, you might have come across this online guide and smartphone app – one that collates together the title listings for a whole load of content services. JustWatch isn’t a TV streaming service itself, though, and you won’t be able to stream anything from within it – but it does offer a handy place to browse everything that is available to stream elsewhere, meaning you don’t have to check apps individually to find what you’re looking for. Let’s face it: there are a lot of TV streaming services these days. While Netflix and YouTube may still be the dominant players when it comes to online streaming, there’s now a host of competitors taking up our screen time. And in a world where Amazon Prime Video , Disney Plus , HBO , and Hulu and are all packed with programming, with content libraries cycling through different titles every month, it can be hard to keep with what’s actually available. That’s where JustWatch comes in – and for everything you need to know about the platform, you’ll find it all on this page. JustWatch is an online guide that collates the various films, TV series, and other types of programming available on online TV streaming services. There’s a website you can open in any browser, and a smartphone app that’s available on iOS and Android , as well as Fire TV devices . This isn’t a new idea: viewers have flocked to the internet to find out what show or film is landing where for years now, but JustWatch is different in its sheer scale. Rather than simply show what’s streaming on a particular service (in the vein of What’sOnNetflix), JustWatch enables you to skim through over 100 different content libraries to see what’s available where, what quality resolution it’s streaming in, how much it costs, and the kind of payment options available (subscription, rental, etc). You can also filter the huge swathes of titles by the following categories: Movies, TV series, Release year, Genres, Price, Rating (i.e. IMDb or Rotten Tomatoes score) and Age rating. This means you can search en masse across various services, rather than simply scouting for a specific title, or having to go into Netflix, Amazon and Hulu separately to see what action movies or animated films are on offer. As the JustWatch smartphone app puts it: “Get personal recommendations for movies and TV shows available on Netflix, Now TV, Disney Plus and many more.” You’ll find well over 100 TV streaming services included on JustWatch, from Netflix and Amazon Prime Video (both rentals / purchases and those included in a Prime subscription) to the likes of Syfy and CBS All Access. Other notable services include DC Universe, Disney Plus, Apple TV Plus, Acorn TV, Rakuten TV, Comedy Central, Hulu, and HBO Max / HBO Now / HBO Go. We won’t list all of them here, but you can head to the JustWatch website to check them out, as each TV streaming service gets an individual icon at the top of the content filters. As to what’s listed for each film or show, you can see when it landed on the respective service, how many episodes are available (if relevant), the streaming quality (SD, HD, 4K ), and how much it costs on each platform for each resolution. You’ll find a run-down of each episode title and synopsis, too, along with the cast and relevant titles you may also want to check out. There’s a watchlist feature, like the kind you get in Netflix or Disney Plus, that lets you tag titles you want to keep a tab on or remember to watch at a later point. You don’t need to log in for this, either, as the information is stored through cookies in your browser – though to get this information across all your devices, you’ll need to make an account (more on this below). Each title has a ‘Watch Now’ button that lets you jump right to the respective platform, too, so you can get right down to streaming. UK residents may be wondering whether your nation-specific catchup services are included. And they are! You’ll find All 4, ITV Hub, BBC iPlayer, and BritBox all on the app. There isn’t, however, a run-down of TV broadcasts, as this is an online-specific guide. Most importantly, JustWatch is free to use. You can make an account for a more tailored user experience – mainly in the form of emails that flag content it thinks you’ll like – but it’s also possible to use without making an account. The About Us page for JustWatch is also surprisingly candid about how it makes its money, stating that user data is used to “collect user profiles of millions of cinema goers” and target them for advertising on behalf of “movie studios, distributors and VOD services”. You’ll find the JustWatch app on iOS and Android smartphones, as well as in internet browsers. If you do sign up, you can do so with your Google or Facebook account, or by inputting an email address and password manually. Note that you will need to accept email marketing when you sign up, though you can head to your account settings after the fact to turn this off. JustWatch is a bit of a no-brainer for heavy TV viewers. It brings together a host of different content libraries, with effective filters and a constantly updated catalogue that reflects the ever-changing libraries of Netflix and the like. You don’t even need to make an account to use it. If you only subscribe or regularly use one or two services, and don’t really fancy checking out any others – that is, if you’re happy to be influenced more by your current subscriptions – it may be more of a hassle than simply searching for Netflix standup specials inside the app itself. What is JustWatch? If you’ve ever scoured the internet to find which TV streaming service has a specific film or series available, you might have come across this online guide and smartphone app – one that collates together the title listings for a whole load of content services.

JustWatch isn’t a TV streaming service itself, though, and you won’t be able to stream anything from within it – but it does offer a handy place to browse everything that is available to stream elsewhere, meaning you don’t have to check apps individually to find what you’re looking for.

Let’s face it: there are a lot of TV streaming services these days. While Netflix and YouTube may still be the dominant players when it comes to online streaming, there’s now a host of competitors taking up our screen time. And in a world where Amazon Prime Video , Disney Plus , HBO , and Hulu and are all packed with programming, with content libraries cycling through different titles every month, it can be hard to keep with what’s actually available.
That’s where JustWatch comes in – and for everything you need to know about the platform, you’ll find it all on this page.

JustWatch is an online guide that collates the various films, TV series, and other types of programming available on online TV streaming services. There’s a website you can open in any browser, and a smartphone app that’s available on iOS and Android , as well as Fire TV devices .

This isn’t a new idea: viewers have flocked to the internet to find out what show or film is landing where for years now, but JustWatch is different in its sheer scale. Rather than simply show what’s streaming on a particular service (in the vein of What’sOnNetflix), JustWatch enables you to skim through over 100 different content libraries to see what’s available where, what quality resolution it’s streaming in, how much it costs, and the kind of payment options available (subscription, rental, etc).
You can also filter the huge swathes of titles by the following categories: Movies, TV series, Release year, Genres, Price, Rating (i.e. IMDb or Rotten Tomatoes score) and Age rating.

This means you can search en masse across various services, rather than simply scouting for a specific title, or having to go into Netflix, Amazon and Hulu separately to see what action movies or animated films are on offer.
As the JustWatch smartphone app puts it: “Get personal recommendations for movies and TV shows available on Netflix, Now TV, Disney Plus and many more.”

You’ll find well over 100 TV streaming services included on JustWatch, from Netflix and Amazon Prime Video (both rentals / purchases and those included in a Prime subscription) to the likes of Syfy and CBS All Access. Other notable services include DC Universe, Disney Plus, Apple TV Plus, Acorn TV, Rakuten TV, Comedy Central, Hulu, and HBO Max / HBO Now / HBO Go.
We won’t list all of them here, but you can head to the JustWatch website to check them out, as each TV streaming service gets an individual icon at the top of the content filters.

As to what’s listed for each film or show, you can see when it landed on the respective service, how many episodes are available (if relevant), the streaming quality (SD, HD, 4K ), and how much it costs on each platform for each resolution. You’ll find a run-down of each episode title and synopsis, too, along with the cast and relevant titles you may also want to check out.

There’s a watchlist feature, like the kind you get in Netflix or Disney Plus, that lets you tag titles you want to keep a tab on or remember to watch at a later point. You don’t need to log in for this, either, as the information is stored through cookies in your browser – though to get this information across all your devices, you’ll need to make an account (more on this below).
Each title has a ‘Watch Now’ button that lets you jump right to the respective platform, too, so you can get right down to streaming.

UK residents may be wondering whether your nation-specific catchup services are included. And they are! You’ll find All 4, ITV Hub, BBC iPlayer, and BritBox all on the app. There isn’t, however, a run-down of TV broadcasts, as this is an online-specific guide.

Most importantly, JustWatch is free to use. You can make an account for a more tailored user experience – mainly in the form of emails that flag content it thinks you’ll like – but it’s also possible to use without making an account.

The About Us page for JustWatch is also surprisingly candid about how it makes its money, stating that user data is used to “collect user profiles of millions of cinema goers” and target them for advertising on behalf of “movie studios, distributors and VOD services”.
You’ll find the JustWatch app on iOS and Android smartphones, as well as in internet browsers.

If you do sign up, you can do so with your Google or Facebook account, or by inputting an email address and password manually. Note that you will need to accept email marketing when you sign up, though you can head to your account settings after the fact to turn this off.

JustWatch is a bit of a no-brainer for heavy TV viewers. It brings together a host of different content libraries, with effective filters and a constantly updated catalogue that reflects the ever-changing libraries of Netflix and the like. You don’t even need to make an account to use it.

If you only subscribe or regularly use one or two services, and don’t really fancy checking out any others – that is, if you’re happy to be influenced more by your current subscriptions – it may be more of a hassle than simply searching for Netflix standup specials inside the app itself.

sources.title: Streaming guide JustWatch becomes a streamer itself
passages: JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself.
On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV.
The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store.
While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service , Howdy.
Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide.

This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others.

“At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners.
Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent.

extraction.body: JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself. On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV. The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store. The media and entertainment company behind the streaming guide, the JustWatch Group, initially announced its plans to venture into streaming last month. At the time, it said partners like Paramount, New Regency, Fremantle, Bleecker Street, and Vortex Media were on board. The company has since announced other content partners, including Cineverse in the U.S., LEONINE Studios in Germany, SND in France, and Altitude in the U.K. The 12-year-old company has long been known for its online guide to movies and TV. Essentially, it’s a “TV Guide” for the streaming era, helping users navigate a landscape where movies and shows move from one service to another, making it harder to keep up with what’s streaming where. Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide. This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others. Now the company believes there’s an even bigger opportunity to grow its audience data and insights by running its own service. “At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners. This is a natural continuation of our mission to contribute to the entire ecosystem, from the big screen to the small one.” The new streaming service will be available within JustWatch’s existing apps and website across 12 markets, including the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Ireland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Australia, and New Zealand. Its free tier will offer a selection of ad-supported titles, while the ad-free version, JustWatch TV Plus, will offer more than 300 ad-free titles in the U.S., as well as other exclusive features, like advanced filters and the option to hide previously seen or disliked titles in the guide. A movie rental store will also initially be available in the U.S., U.K., Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, with more markets to follow in time. While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service , Howdy. It will be similarly priced at $3.99 per month or $49.99 for a lifetime subscription. (The latter is an interesting way to price streaming, given the evolving content costs, but JustWatch believes there will be additional value in the data collected.) Paid subscribers will also be able to take 10% off on hundreds of rentals in the JustWatch TV Store, the company noted. Like most low-cost services, JustWatch’s content lineup focuses on older movies and shows, as well as more indie content. Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent. JustWatch says users will be able to request titles they want to see to help shape what comes to the service. However, if you want to watch something epic without dishing out the big bucks, then free streamers like Hoopla , Plex , and Pluto will be your best bet.
To take out some of the guesswork that follows, here are the 10 best fantasy movies streaming for free right now.
Movies are the best type of escapism, and when you truly want to disappear into a fictional world for a bit, no genre is better than fantasy.
However, the next question becomes how do you watch them on streaming.
The movie follows one unicorn's desperate search to discover what happened to the rest of her species, and what follows is a story packed with themes about mortality, existential fear, and regret.
For these reasons, it's best suited for older kids and adults.
This isn't My Little Pony (1986), meaning young children might have difficulty processing these mature themes despite the G-rating.
Want a fantasy movie that you can watch with the whole family?
While 1987's Masters of the Universe isn't necessarily topping many critically acclaimed "best of" lists, it's still a great pick for those who dig "so-bad-they're-good" movies.

The costume and set designs are actually quite impressive.
Plus, Frank Langella is having one heck of a good time playing Skeletor.
With a new He-Man film slated for release in June 2026, it's the perfect time to revisit the first live-action adaptation of Mattel's favorite toyline hero turned movie and TV star.
44 other streaming services also have titles available to stream today.

Monty Python and the Holy Grail isn't the movie to watch when you're craving a serious fantasy movie.
Told in a non-linear fashion with some genuinely impressive transitions between time periods, the movie offers a compelling time-travel story steeped in action and fantasy.
The proof is in the pudding, with director Matteo Garrone—a lifelong fan of Carlo Collodi's original fairy tale—producing a critically acclaimed, award-winning film.
The daydreaming sequences are fun, whimsical, and utterly theatrical.

passages: Movies are the best type of escapism, and when you truly want to disappear into a fictional world for a bit, no genre is better than fantasy. Whether it's the grandeur of medieval-set tales, the epic slashing of clashing swords, or the dark forests in fairy tales reimagined, fantasy excels at immersion. You'll want to get lost in these worlds, and who can really blame you? However, the next question becomes how do you watch them on streaming.

With no shortage of streaming services available these days, fantasy movies exist in the libraries of all of them. However, if you want to watch something epic without dishing out the big bucks, then free streamers like Hoopla , Plex , and Pluto will be your best bet. To take out some of the guesswork that follows, here are the 10 best fantasy movies streaming for free right now.

Monty Python and the Holy Grail isn't the movie to watch when you're craving a serious fantasy movie. As a parody of Arthurian legend, this one is for fantasy fans who don't mind comedy aimed at the genre's tropes and clichés. Don't expect historical accuracy; if anything, prepare yourself for the wonkiest quest for the Holy Grail in all of film, littered with absurd and hilarious scenes.

Those familiar with Monty Python or the comedy group's other movies, like Life of Brian (1979), will feel right at home with the witty British humor often disguised beneath seemingly stupid jokes. This movie is quotable, so lock in and prepare to hurl all manner of iconic lines at your friends and family for the foreseeable future.

If action-heavy sword and sorcery fare is your weakness, you really can't do much better than Highlander .

coreStoryFacts.text: If you’ve ever scoured the internet to find which TV streaming service has a specific film or series available, you might have come across this online guide and smartphone app – one that collates together the title listings for a whole load of content services.
There’s a website you can open in any browser, and a smartphone app that’s available on iOS and Android , as well as Fire TV devices .
Other notable services include DC Universe, Disney Plus, Apple TV Plus, Acorn TV, Rakuten TV, Comedy Central, Hulu, and HBO Max / HBO Now / HBO Go.
Unlock and manage exclusive Techradar member rewards.

The About Us page for JustWatch is also surprisingly candid about how it makes its money, stating that user data is used to “collect user profiles of millions of cinema goers” and target them for advertising on behalf of “movie studios, distributors and VOD services”.
JustWatch is a bit of a no-brainer for heavy TV viewers.
It brings together a host of different content libraries, with effective filters and a constantly updated catalogue that reflects the ever-changing libraries of Netflix and the like.
You don’t even need to make an account to use it.

Other bylines include Edge, T3, iMore, GamesRadar, NBC News, Healthline, and The Times.
TechRadar is part of Future US Inc, an international media group and leading digital publisher.
JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself.
On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV.
The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store.
While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service , Howdy.
Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide.

This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others.

“At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners.
Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent.

If you’ve ever scoured the internet to find which TV streaming service has a specific film or series available, you might have come across this online guide and smartphone app – one that collates together the title listings for a whole load of content services. JustWatch isn’t a TV streaming service itself, though, and you won’t be able to stream anything from within it – but it does offer a handy place to browse everything that is available to stream elsewhere, meaning you don’t have to check apps individually to find what you’re looking for. Let’s face it: there are a lot of TV streaming services these days. While Netflix and YouTube may still be the dominant players when it comes to online streaming, there’s now a host of competitors taking up our screen time. And in a world where Amazon Prime Video , Disney Plus , HBO , and Hulu and are all packed with programming, with content libraries cycling through different titles every month, it can be hard to keep with what’s actually available. That’s where JustWatch comes in – and for everything you need to know about the platform, you’ll find it all on this page. JustWatch is an online guide that collates the various films, TV series, and other types of programming available on online TV streaming services. There’s a website you can open in any browser, and a smartphone app that’s available on iOS and Android , as well as Fire TV devices . This isn’t a new idea: viewers have flocked to the internet to find out what show or film is landing where for years now, but JustWatch is different in its sheer scale. Rather than simply show what’s streaming on a particular service (in the vein of What’sOnNetflix), JustWatch enables you to skim through over 100 different content libraries to see what’s available where, what quality resolution it’s streaming in, how much it costs, and the kind of payment options available (subscription, rental, etc). You can also filter the huge swathes of titles by the following categories: Movies, TV series, Release year, Genres, Price, Rating (i.e. IMDb or Rotten Tomatoes score) and Age rating. This means you can search en masse across various services, rather than simply scouting for a specific title, or having to go into Netflix, Amazon and Hulu separately to see what action movies or animated films are on offer. As the JustWatch smartphone app puts it: “Get personal recommendations for movies and TV shows available on Netflix, Now TV, Disney Plus and many more.” You’ll find well over 100 TV streaming services included on JustWatch, from Netflix and Amazon Prime Video (both rentals / purchases and those included in a Prime subscription) to the likes of Syfy and CBS All Access. Other notable services include DC Universe, Disney Plus, Apple TV Plus, Acorn TV, Rakuten TV, Comedy Central, Hulu, and HBO Max / HBO Now / HBO Go. We won’t list all of them here, but you can head to the JustWatch website to check them out, as each TV streaming service gets an individual icon at the top of the content filters. As to what’s listed for each film or show, you can see when it landed on the respective service, how many episodes are available (if relevant), the streaming quality (SD, HD, 4K ), and how much it costs on each platform for each resolution. You’ll find a run-down of each episode title and synopsis, too, along with the cast and relevant titles you may also want to check out. There’s a watchlist feature, like the kind you get in Netflix or Disney Plus, that lets you tag titles you want to keep a tab on or remember to watch at a later point. You don’t need to log in for this, either, as the information is stored through cookies in your browser – though to get this information across all your devices, you’ll need to make an account (more on this below). Each title has a ‘Watch Now’ button that lets you jump right to the respective platform, too, so you can get right down to streaming. UK residents may be wondering whether your nation-specific catchup services are included. And they are! You’ll find All 4, ITV Hub, BBC iPlayer, and BritBox all on the app. There isn’t, however, a run-down of TV broadcasts, as this is an online-specific guide. Most importantly, JustWatch is free to use. You can make an account for a more tailored user experience – mainly in the form of emails that flag content it thinks you’ll like – but it’s also possible to use without making an account. The About Us page for JustWatch is also surprisingly candid about how it makes its money, stating that user data is used to “collect user profiles of millions of cinema goers” and target them for advertising on behalf of “movie studios, distributors and VOD services”. You’ll find the JustWatch app on iOS and Android smartphones, as well as in internet browsers. If you do sign up, you can do so with your Google or Facebook account, or by inputting an email address and password manually. Note that you will need to accept email marketing when you sign up, though you can head to your account settings after the fact to turn this off. JustWatch is a bit of a no-brainer for heavy TV viewers. It brings together a host of different content libraries, with effective filters and a constantly updated catalogue that reflects the ever-changing libraries of Netflix and the like. You don’t even need to make an account to use it. If you only subscribe or regularly use one or two services, and don’t really fancy checking out any others – that is, if you’re happy to be influenced more by your current subscriptions – it may be more of a hassle than simply searching for Netflix standup specials inside the app itself. extraction.body: JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself. On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV. The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store. The media and entertainment company behind the streaming guide, the JustWatch Group, initially announced its plans to venture into streaming last month. At the time, it said partners like Paramount, New Regency, Fremantle, Bleecker Street, and Vortex Media were on board. The company has since announced other content partners, including Cineverse in the U.S., LEONINE Studios in Germany, SND in France, and Altitude in the U.K. The 12-year-old company has long been known for its online guide to movies and TV. Essentially, it’s a “TV Guide” for the streaming era, helping users navigate a landscape where movies and shows move from one service to another, making it harder to keep up with what’s streaming where. Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide. This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others. Now the company believes there’s an even bigger opportunity to grow its audience data and insights by running its own service. “At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners. This is a natural continuation of our mission to contribute to the entire ecosystem, from the big screen to the small one.” The new streaming service will be available within JustWatch’s existing apps and website across 12 markets, including the U.S., Canada, the U.K., Ireland, Germany, Austria, France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Australia, and New Zealand. Its free tier will offer a selection of ad-supported titles, while the ad-free version, JustWatch TV Plus, will offer more than 300 ad-free titles in the U.S., as well as other exclusive features, like advanced filters and the option to hide previously seen or disliked titles in the guide. A movie rental store will also initially be available in the U.S., U.K., Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand, with more markets to follow in time. While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service , Howdy. It will be similarly priced at $3.99 per month or $49.99 for a lifetime subscription. (The latter is an interesting way to price streaming, given the evolving content costs, but JustWatch believes there will be additional value in the data collected.) Paid subscribers will also be able to take 10% off on hundreds of rentals in the JustWatch TV Store, the company noted. Like most low-cost services, JustWatch’s content lineup focuses on older movies and shows, as well as more indie content. Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent. JustWatch says users will be able to request titles they want to see to help shape what comes to the service. relevantPassages.text: JustWatch, a company offering a search engine and guide for streaming movies and TV shows, is now moving directly into the streaming business itself.
On Tuesday, the company behind the popular guide that’s used by 50 million people is launching JustWatch TV.
The new streaming service will feature content from 30 partners and will offer both free and paid tiers, as well as a movie rental store.
While the ad-supported tier competes with free streamers like Tubi and Plex, the Plus tier will compete with low-cost streamers like Roku’s $2.99 per month ad-free service , Howdy.
Available in 140 markets globally, the guide provides streaming options for more than 500,000 movies and shows across more than 1,500 service providers worldwide.

This “where to watch” information and streaming chart data are also used to power some 1,400 partner websites and apps and are valuable to studios, distributors, streamers, and agencies that use the data to target their campaigns across social media platforms like Meta, YouTube, TikTok, and others.

“At a time where there is so much choice, yet with so many people constantly searching for a place to find their favourite film, the series they just heard about, or something exciting that fits them, it is a great moment to be a hub for all things entertainment,” said Quentin Carbonell, JustWatch SVP of Global Content Acquisitions and Strategy, in an email shared with TechCrunch. “By having our own service with titles to watch directly on JustWatch TV, we can grow our already massive audience, while continuing to direct them to all our streaming partners.
Another unique feature is that users will be able to influence the service’s content to some extent.

extraction.body: J.P. Morgan announced on October 19 that its Kinexys business had brought JPM Coin (JPMD), its US dollar-denominated deposit token, to Ethereum mainnet for institutional clients. Confirmed in a company announcement , the deployment expands JPM Coin’s availability beyond Base, giving approved participants another public blockchain for moving tokenized deposits. JPM Coin remains a permissioned product restricted to approved institutional participants rather than a retail-accessible crypto asset, according to Cointelegraph. The Ethereum deployment places JPM Coin on the network where a broad range of assets, collateral arrangements and counterparties already operate onchain. It gives clients another public-chain option for near-real-time, around-the-clock money movement, according to Bloomberg Law . JPM Coin is denominated in US dollars and represents deposits within J.P. Morgan’s system. The announcement concerns its availability on Ethereum mainnet for institutional clients; it does not signal an opening of the token to the general public. J.P. Morgan said JPM Coin supports peer-to-peer transfers between institutional clients in the Ethereum Virtual Machine ecosystem, including Ethereum and Base. The bank described the arrangement as an onchain liquidity layer for USD deposits. That framing focuses on settlement between eligible institutions operating across those networks. Access is restricted to approved institutional participants, a limitation reported by Cointelegraph , rather than an unrestricted token offering on Ethereum. The Ethereum rollout follows JPM Coin’s November 2025 launch on Base. The expansion brings the bank’s deposit-token infrastructure to a second public blockchain while retaining the approved-participant model. Kinexys has processed more than $4 trillion in cumulative transactions since inception and has averaged $7 billion in daily transaction volume, according to J.P. Morgan. Confirmed in a company announcement , the deployment expands JPM Coin’s availability beyond Base, giving approved participants another public blockchain for moving tokenized deposits. JPM Coin remains a permissioned product restricted to approved institutional participants rather than a retail-accessible crypto asset, according to Cointelegraph. The Ethereum deployment places JPM Coin on the network where a broad range of assets, collateral arrangements and counterparties already operate onchain. It gives clients another public-chain option for near-real-time, around-the-clock money movement, according to Bloomberg Law . JPM Coin is denominated in US dollars and represents deposits within J.P. Morgan’s system. The announcement concerns its availability on Ethereum mainnet for institutional clients; it does not signal an opening of the token to the general public. J.P. Morgan said JPM Coin supports peer-to-peer transfers between institutional clients in the Ethereum Virtual Machine ecosystem, including Ethereum and Base. The bank described the arrangement as an onchain liquidity layer for USD deposits. That framing focuses on settlement between eligible institutions operating across those networks. Access is restricted to approved institutional participants, a limitation reported by Cointelegraph , rather than an unrestricted token offering on Ethereum. The Ethereum rollout follows JPM Coin’s November 2025 launch on Base. The expansion brings the bank’s deposit-token infrastructure to a second public blockchain while retaining the approved-participant model. Kinexys has processed more than $4 trillion in cumulative transactions since inception and has averaged $7 billion in daily transaction volume, according to J.P. Morgan. “A tokenized security digitizes ownership or economic rights associated with an asset. A tokenized deposit represents commercial-bank money and remains a liability of the issuing bank,” the report said. “A stablecoin typically represents a claim structured separately from a traditional commercial-bank deposit and is designed to circulate more broadly, often across public blockchain networks.”

JPMorgan, the report added, offers what is perhaps the clearest example of how far production infrastructure can extend past experimentation. Kinexys said in April that its blockchain-based infrastructure had processed upwards of $3 trillion since launching and was averaging more than $5 billion in transactions each day.

PYMNTS wrote Monday about research from PYMNTS Intelligence showing that digital wallets might be an effective way for credit unions to get their members interested in stablecoins and cryptocurrency .

“A familiar wallet can work like a familiar dashboard in a new car, making an unfamiliar experience easier to navigate,” the report said. “For credit unions, the findings suggest that how members access digital assets deserves attention alongside which assets they offer.”

extraction.body: Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it investigates its privacy. Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: “If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.” In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said: We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered. Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way. The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database. Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible. “Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.” Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended. Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires. With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed.

Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including:
“If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.”
In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said:

We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered.

Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way.

The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database.

Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible.

“Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.”

Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended.

Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires.
With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now.

Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

passages: But Shinn said on an episode of "Invest Like The Best" in late September that the invite-only service has been growing by roughly 10% a day and is processing more than $1 billion in annualized transaction volume, despite what he called a "very small user base." But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information.
For some, blunders and privacy scares from their agents have proven too unnerving.

Four early adopters, among dozens of people raising similar concerns on social media, told Business Insider they had deleted or restricted personal AI agents over concerns about the sensitive data and account access the tools need to work effectively.

Users have reported agents accessing one-time login codes from Gmail without asking, hallucinating personal information from a document that was never sent, and triggering a carrier-account login prompt apparently originating from Iran.
"I have no clue where my data is going and what kind of privacy I do get from using that agent," Martino said.

It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.
Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them.

Muse shot to the top of the App Store a week after launch, and it continues to attract users.

For some, blunders and privacy scares from their agents have proven too unnerving. Four early adopters, among dozens of people raising similar concerns on social media, told Business Insider they had deleted or restricted personal AI agents over concerns about the sensitive data and account access the tools need to work effectively. Guto Martino, a cofounder of Hermes Agents Brasil, a community that helps people build and run open-source personal AI agents, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct because he was unsure how the company handled his information. "I have no clue where my data is going and what kind of privacy I do get from using that agent," Martino said. Martino's decision follows a string of troubling episodes involving personal AI agents. Users have reported agents accessing one-time login codes from Gmail without asking, hallucinating personal information from a document that was never sent, and triggering a carrier-account login prompt apparently originating from Iran. Meta said Muse has "first-of-its-kind privacy, safety, and security protections" and that its controls put users in charge of what they share. It said users choose which apps Muse connects to and what it can do with services such as email, and can change or remove access, or permanently delete their Muse data. While a handful of users are wary, vastly more are experimenting with the technology. Muse shot to the top of the App Store a week after launch, and it continues to attract users. The Information reported that Meta's Muse now has more than 3 million weekly users, including more than 1 million daily active users. But Shinn said on an episode of "Invest Like The Best" in late September that the invite-only service has been growing by roughly 10% a day and is processing more than $1 billion in annualized transaction volume, despite what he called a "very small user base." But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information. Scott Persinger, the CTO of AI-powered travel platform BizTrip, told Business Insider he found Instinct "very cool," but deleted it because he was not prepared to let a young startup handle his personal email. "Access to email is everything — via password resets you could probably access my whole life," he said. He said he still uses Meta's Muse and xAI's Grok Bot, though neither is connected to his inbox. "I fully expect to use a personal assistant with my email," Persinger said. "But I want to hear someone describe how they built it safely, not just 'yolo — trust us.'" Muse users weren't spared. Rami Elghandour, chairman and CEO of Arcellx, a clinical-stage biotechnology company, told Business Insider he deleted Muse after reading reports that the agent had accessed users' text messages without permission. Elghandour had used Muse to search for a new Mac Studio and a car, but said he had deliberately not connected it to any accounts or personal data. "The fact that it was accessing user text messages without their consent was alarming but not surprising given it's Meta," Elghandour said. "I certainly did not grant or would I ever grant access to all my messages to Meta." He said he instead uses an agent he built himself with an open-source model on a Mac Mini, which has access to his email, calendar, and messages. "I’m not sure I would give that level of access to any company," he said. Mahesh Vellanki, the founder and CEO of YieldClub, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct after it triggered a two-factor authentication request from an IP location labeled as Iran while trying to log into his carrier account. He said Instinct suggested it could have been a benign IP-tagging issue, and he could not establish that its systems were compromised. Still, the episode left him feeling "very exposed." Vellanki said he still uses personal AI agents, but no longer gives them sensitive information. "More just using them generally, but not giving them full keys to the castle," he said. "It’s the wild west with these products," he added. Not every early user worried about their personal data has chosen to abandon personal AI agents. Rishi Bhargava, cofounder of Descope, said he is experimenting with Muse and Instinct but has been "very careful" about the access he gives them, including by withholding his passwords. He said he uses Instinct only for lower-stakes tasks, such as search and research. "The interface is extremely convenient, and I like the asynchronous nature of it," he said. But Bhargava said companies behind personal AI agents have not adequately explained how they handle and protect personal data. Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them. It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.

extraction.body: Meta is suspending the sharing feature while it investigates its privacy. Muse, the new general-purpose AI agent from Meta, can expose sensitive information when users share conversations through web links, researchers reported Monday. In response to questions from Ars about the behavior, Meta said it’s suspending the sharing feature while the company reviews it and considers making changes. Like many online services, Muse has allowed users to share searches, conversations, images, and similar content with other people. Such share features usually involve clicking an option to create a unique URL that anyone can use to load a page hosting the content. To keep potentially sensitive information from being accessible to unintended people, the URLs typically contain a long sequence of text that can’t be easily guessed. Muse, which Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said last month was “built from the ground up for privacy and security,” seems to take the same precautions. But a central design decision for constructing URLs has made the links easy to discover. As a result, researchers from security firm Claroc said they were able to enumerate 6,800 links Muse users created for sharing conversations with others. After opening a few hundred of them, the researchers found information that was clearly not intended to be publicly available, including: “If you had asked us beforehand, we would have guessed that gathering these would take real effort,” the researchers wrote. “It took one query.” In an emailed statement responding to questions from Ars, Meta said: We opened the Muse bug bounty program so researchers could raise different scenarios and help us continue improving the product. People have the ability to share specific Muse artifacts, which creates a page that can be accessed by those with the link. However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered. Asaf Aprozper, the co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he reported the findings through Meta’s bug bounty program on October 8 and also tried reaching people at Meta on LinkedIn, but got no reply either way. The easiest way to discover the URLs is to perform a passive DNS search through one of many available commercial services. Passive DNS records store the historical resolution of domain names to IP addresses, as well as nameserver, and mail-server records over time. Passive DNS systems typically collect DNS responses from sensors positioned at recursive DNS resolvers or other infrastructure. A passive DNS record is generally created when a monitoring system observes a DNS response. In the case here, once the intended party clicks on the share link, the DNS information is recorded in a searchable database. Claroc researchers were able to discover the Muse share links because all of them use the domain name cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Discovery is further made easy by the decision to add the conversation name to the URL, along with a long string of text. Simplified examples of such links are home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, q3-revenue-review-7b1e42f0.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, and loan-application-draft-a4c9e2.cf.metaaiusercontent.com. It’s this last design decision, putting the conversation title in the subdomain rather than in the URL path, that makes public discovery possible. “Plenty of AI assistants share by public link,” Claroc said. “What makes Muse’s shares easy to find is the title sitting inside the web address, where public DNS records it for anyone to search. We call these GhostShares: pages that open for people who were never handed the link, and that those people can find on their own.” Muse quickly catapulted to one of the top spots in Apple’s App Store. The assistant autonomously fills out forms, books appointments, makes purchases, creates documents, and carries out all kinds of other actions. To work as intended, Muse requires access to most of a user’s accounts. Meta has heavily marketed the assistant as a platform that’s worthy of the extraordinary trust it needs to work as intended. Three weeks after the Muse launch, macOS security expert Patrick Wardle discovered a zero-day vulnerability that allowed any other app installed on the same device to gain complete control of the user’s Muse account. Meta downplayed the severity of the vulnerability on the grounds that exploitation wasn’t possible unless a device was already compromised. The company didn’t acknowledge Wardle’s finding that a simple ClickFix attack was all that was needed to hijack an account. The ease in discovering share links further justifies asking if Muse is worthy of the access it requires. With Meta’s suspension of the feature, Muse users no longer face this particular threat, at least for now. Ars Technica has been separating the signal from the noise for over 25 years. With our unique combination of technical savvy and wide-ranging interest in the technological arts and sciences, Ars is the trusted source in a sea of information. After all, you don’t need to know everything, only what’s important.

extraction.body: Many early adopters of Instinct and Meta's Muse have said the digital assistants saved them time and money by searching the web, managing inboxes and calendars, disputing bills, booking travel, and making purchases. Four early adopters, among dozens of people raising similar concerns on social media, told Business Insider they had deleted or restricted personal AI agents over concerns about the sensitive data and account access the tools need to work effectively. Guto Martino, a cofounder of Hermes Agents Brasil, a community that helps people build and run open-source personal AI agents, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct because he was unsure how the company handled his information. "I have no clue where my data is going and what kind of privacy I do get from using that agent," Martino said. Martino's decision follows a string of troubling episodes involving personal AI agents. Users have reported agents accessing one-time login codes from Gmail without asking, hallucinating personal information from a document that was never sent, and triggering a carrier-account login prompt apparently originating from Iran. Meta said Muse has "first-of-its-kind privacy, safety, and security protections" and that its controls put users in charge of what they share. It said users choose which apps Muse connects to and what it can do with services such as email, and can change or remove access, or permanently delete their Muse data. While a handful of users are wary, vastly more are experimenting with the technology. Muse shot to the top of the App Store a week after launch, and it continues to attract users. The Information reported that Meta's Muse now has more than 3 million weekly users, including more than 1 million daily active users. But Shinn said on an episode of "Invest Like The Best" in late September that the invite-only service has been growing by roughly 10% a day and is processing more than $1 billion in annualized transaction volume, despite what he called a "very small user base." But for those who aren't sure about agents, it often comes down to a simple trade-off: Personal AI agents require broad access to your inboxes, calendars, payment methods, and other accounts that contain highly sensitive information. Scott Persinger, the CTO of AI-powered travel platform BizTrip, told Business Insider he found Instinct "very cool," but deleted it because he was not prepared to let a young startup handle his personal email. "Access to email is everything — via password resets you could probably access my whole life," he said. He said he still uses Meta's Muse and xAI's Grok Bot, though neither is connected to his inbox. "I fully expect to use a personal assistant with my email," Persinger said. "But I want to hear someone describe how they built it safely, not just 'yolo — trust us.'" Muse users weren't spared. Rami Elghandour, chairman and CEO of Arcellx, a clinical-stage biotechnology company, told Business Insider he deleted Muse after reading reports that the agent had accessed users' text messages without permission. Elghandour had used Muse to search for a new Mac Studio and a car, but said he had deliberately not connected it to any accounts or personal data. "The fact that it was accessing user text messages without their consent was alarming but not surprising given it's Meta," Elghandour said. "I certainly did not grant or would I ever grant access to all my messages to Meta." He said he instead uses an agent he built himself with an open-source model on a Mac Mini, which has access to his email, calendar, and messages. "I’m not sure I would give that level of access to any company," he said. Deleted Muse after seeing this post on Threads about how it told some Facebook Marketplace sellers the guy’s address and they showed up at his doorDangerous and creepyThis would have been 1000x worse if the person was a woman pic.twitter.com/KQbkwRzDPt For others, the potential for data leaks was the last straw. Mahesh Vellanki, the founder and CEO of YieldClub, told Business Insider he deleted Instinct after it triggered a two-factor authentication request from an IP location labeled as Iran while trying to log into his carrier account. He said Instinct suggested it could have been a benign IP-tagging issue, and he could not establish that its systems were compromised. Still, the episode left him feeling "very exposed." Vellanki said he still uses personal AI agents, but no longer gives them sensitive information. "More just using them generally, but not giving them full keys to the castle," he said. "It’s the wild west with these products," he added. Not every early user worried about their personal data has chosen to abandon personal AI agents. Rishi Bhargava, cofounder of Descope, said he is experimenting with Muse and Instinct but has been "very careful" about the access he gives them, including by withholding his passwords. He said he uses Instinct only for lower-stakes tasks, such as search and research. "The interface is extremely convenient, and I like the asynchronous nature of it," he said. But Bhargava said companies behind personal AI agents have not adequately explained how they handle and protect personal data. Instinct says users can disconnect their Google accounts and delete the data it collected from them. It also says it does not use Google Workspace data to train its AI models or show ads, but warns that no system is completely secure and that users should review the agent's actions.

extraction.body: Justin Mast’s life was changed by a cyborg plant. A few years ago, Mast was reading through some scientific literature when he stumbled upon research about a houseplant wired to a motorized stand . When the plant wanted more light, electrical signals flowed through the living tissues. A control board sensed the current and wheeled the plant closer to the light source. “I’m like, what the heck?” Mast told TechCrunch. “That was the entry to the rabbit hole for me.” Mast wound up partnering with Lee von Kraus, a neuroscientist who has worked with DARPA, to found Electric Plant , which has been spending the past three years collecting data to build a large language model, Bombadil, capable of interpreting the subtle electrical signals coursing through a plant’s stem and relaying details about the plant’s needs to growers. The founders believe their model could one day lead to a tool that would let people “speak” to plants. “We’re listening more than we’re speaking, but listening’s the first step,” said Mast, co-founder and CEO of Electric Plant. To bring its sensors and Bombadil to market, Electric Plant recently raised an $11.2 million seed round led by Onto Ventures and Climactic, with participation from Ponderosa, Endeavor Catalyst, Ludlow, Michigan Rise, The Fund, Schox VC, and Dug Song. Even in the most controlled greenhouses, farmers and growers don’t have full visibility of what their plants require, Mast said. Traditionally, farmers, growers, and foresters have relied on coarse tools that react to plants’ demands for water, nutrients, or light. And tools like soil probes, handheld spectroscopes, and satellite imagery work well enough, but they leave much to be desired, Mast said. “That technology is sophisticated, but its ability to get at the inside of the plant isn’t very sophisticated. Most of that stuff still lags quite a bit behind the real-time needs of the plant,” he said. Electric Plant had to start somewhere, though, so it used those devices to train its Bombadil model, which is capable of interpreting electrical signals in about 125 different species. “We know the model will surpass a lot of that equipment,” Mast said. The startup’s sensors are also significantly cheaper than existing tools, which generally cost thousands of dollars. “This is tens of dollars,” he said. The sensors, about the size of a regular iPhone folded lengthwise, are attached to a plant using stainless steel screws. The screws must penetrate the cambium — the layer of living tissue just under the bark — to connect to the microvolt changes occurring within the plant. Data collected from these sensors is sent to a base station via a low-power wireless network. Electric Plant only needs a couple sensors per acre for accurate results, Mast said. The data gets interpreted by Bombadil in the cloud, and the results are sent back to the customer, who can use it to, for example, adjust their watering or fertilizer schedules. Mast claims such a system can boost yields while reducing water use by 20% or more. Mast wouldn’t disclose who Electric Plant’s initial customers are, but it’s easy to imagine applications in agriculture and forestry. Bombadil’s first hundred-plus species runs the gamut of plant forms, from ferns, redwoods, and tomatoes to dahlias, Mast said. “This is the most diverse model ever created on biological electrical signals,” he said. “No one’s ever done anything equivalent to this in the animal world.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . TerraPower has explored simpler, cheaper reactors since 2008 and expects to complete the new reactor in 2030. “I put in over a billion, and I’ll put in billions more,” said Gates, the world’s sixth-richest person according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. TerraPower’s plant, which has backing by the US Department of Energy, was initially expected to be operational in 2028. But that would have meant relying on fuel from Russia, which is “unacceptable now,” Gates said on CNN’s Fareed Zakaria GPS . The reactor design uses liquid sodium as a coolant rather than water and includes molten salt that can store heat to boost its output. TerraPower plans to source reactor fuel from the US and its allies, Gates said. “Coal is being outcompeted by natural gas,” Gates told CNN. “And so what we have to do is compete effectively with natural gas.” Carbon-free nuclear power is increasingly seen as a key part of fighting climate change, and more companies are promoting smaller reactors. Last year, 25 nations at the COP28 climate change conference in Dubai declared an ambition to triple nuclear capacity, according to BloombergNEF.
