passages: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys
Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards.

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.”

The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections.
Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.
Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 .
In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account.
Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

“If Barclaycard doesn't want to lend money to crypto traders, that's up to them,” he said. “They need to manage their own risk as they see fit, and they make a good point that crypto losses are never covered by the financial services compensation scheme.”
However, Goodman added that it really “annoys” him when UK banks refuse to let people send their own money from their own bank account to a crypto trading account.
“And that happens more often than you might think," he adds.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.
Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved.

"Experienced crypto traders often borrow money to trade, just as advanced stock market traders do,” he says. “But it takes skill to manage your risk sensibly and a lot of traders go broke when they get it wrong.”

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.” The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections. Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit. Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.” The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022. Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 . In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account. Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card. This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money. “If Barclaycard doesn't want to lend money to crypto traders, that's up to them,” he said. “They need to manage their own risk as they see fit, and they make a good point that crypto losses are never covered by the financial services compensation scheme.” However, Goodman added that it really “annoys” him when UK banks refuse to let people send their own money from their own bank account to a crypto trading account. “And that happens more often than you might think," he adds. Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively. Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved. passages: Barclays Joins List of UK Banks Restricting Credit Card Crypto Buys
Barclays has joined a growing list of UK banks imposing restrictions on crypto transactions after blocking its customers from purchasing cryptocurrencies with their credit cards.

Announcing the move on its Barclaycard website, Barclays said , “From 27 June 2025, we’ll block crypto-transactions made with a Barclaycard because we recognise there are certain risks with purchasing crypto-currencies.”

The bank went on to explain that it has imposed the block because a decline in cryptocurrency prices could land its customers in debt, while adding that digital assets aren’t covered by existing banking and financial protections.
Barclays move comes after reports that the UK’s financial regulator, the Financial Conduct Authority, is seeking to introduce a blanket ban on all cryptocurrency purchases involving credit.

Outlining its concerns in a discussion paper , the FCA said, “We are concerned that consumers buying crypto assets with credit may take on unsustainable debt, particularly if the value of their crypto asset drops and they were relying on its value to repay.”

The same paper also cited a YouGov survey which found that 14% of UK-based cryptocurrency investors had used some kind of credit card or credit facility to purchase crypto as of August 2024, up from 6% in August 2022.
Barclays decision to stop its customers using their credit cards for cryptocurrency transactions also comes after similar moves by Chase UK, HSBC and Nationwide in 2023 .
In Nationwide’s case, it set a £5,000 (approximately $6,860) spending limit on crypto payments using debit cards, which come directly from a customer’s checking account.
Going even further, Chase UK prevented its customers from making any kind of transaction to cryptocurrency exchanges and services, whether from a customer’s credit or debit card.

This crosses a line for some cryptocurrency experts, with analyst and author Glen Goodman telling Decrypt that, while he can sympathize with a bank stopping the use of credit for crypto purchases, he doesn’t think it’s right that it can stop someone from spending their own money.

“If Barclaycard doesn't want to lend money to crypto traders, that's up to them,” he said. “They need to manage their own risk as they see fit, and they make a good point that crypto losses are never covered by the financial services compensation scheme.”
However, Goodman added that it really “annoys” him when UK banks refuse to let people send their own money from their own bank account to a crypto trading account.
“And that happens more often than you might think," he adds.

Indeed, some UK banks—such as Barclays and Lloyds —have prevented transfers of any kind to Binance for several years now, while TSB and Santander have banned all crypto purchases since 2021 and 2022, respectively.
Despite regarding such actions as examples of overreach, Goodman does caution against using debt to trade cryptocurrency, given the risks involved.

"Experienced crypto traders often borrow money to trade, just as advanced stock market traders do,” he says. “But it takes skill to manage your risk sensibly and a lot of traders go broke when they get it wrong.”

sources.title: Google has joined Amazon in attacking Nvidia’s stronghold with AI app developers
passages: None of this means AI app developers will automatically ditch Nvidia’s hardware en masse just because they can now easily move to alternative chips and clouds.
On Tuesday, Google announced that TorchTPU, its long-awaited version of PyTorch, is now available as an open-source project.
TorchNeuron allows AI apps to be ported to Amazon’s homegrown AI chip, Trainium, and to AWS with no rewriting.
Google may be one-upping Amazon in a few ways, however.

It says it worked directly with Meta, Hugging Face, Inferact (maker of vLLM) RadixArk (maker of SGLang), and others to ensure that TorchTPU’s features and code libraries work well with these popular AI development tools, just as the original PyTorch does.
It even updated its popular LiteRT tool, which runs AI on phones, laptops and embedded devices, to work better with PyTorch AI apps.
It is, by some accounts, used by 85% of the AI apps.
PyTorch was originally developed by Meta (then Facebook) in 2016, long before the world had an inkling that LLMs would change the world.
At the time, Nvidia’s GPUs were already the standard hardware for AI research, so many of PyTorch’s features were built to work specifically with them.
In 2022, Meta turned PyTorch over to the Linux Foundation, a nonprofit that manages many important open source projects.
It also makes it easy to move existing PyTorch apps to TPUs and, therefore, to Google Cloud.
Developers can do this with a simple configuration change and no re-writing of their apps.

sources.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub - MIT Technology Review
passages: Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor.
To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea.
Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online.
Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air.

And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips.
